Volume 32, Supplement –Summer 2026 SUPPLEMENT ISSUE Other Monkeypox Virus Surveillance in Wastewater, North Carolina, USA, October 2023–May 2025 Cite This Article Citation for Media Abstract In September 2023, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services identified a new case of mpox clade II 5 months after the last previous report. To assess possible unrecognized transmission, nonvariola orthopoxvirus testing was implemented at select wastewater sites. During October 29, 2023–May 2025, a total of 801 samples were collected across 16 treatment plants serving ≈2 million residents. We analyzed wastewater detections (n = 47) and clinical cases (n = 45) using a +17-day window. Overall sensitivity of identifying the presence of >1 temporally aligned mpox case within a sewershed was 10.6% (95% CI 6.5%–16.7%); specificity was 95.1% (95% CI 93.2%–96.5%), positive predictive value was 31.9% (95% CI 20.4%–46.2%), and negative predictive value was 83.2% (95% CI 80.3%–85.7%). Restricting detections above the limit of detection reduced sensitivity but increased specificity. Overall, wastewater surveillance showed low sensitivity but provided complementary awareness for public health response. Since the first case was identified in a nonendemic region, mpox has emerged as an increasing public health concern in the United States. The global outbreak in 2022 affected 75 countries and territories; >2,300 cases had been confirmed in the United States by July 2022 (1). Because of evolving transmission dynamics, severity, and uncertainty surrounding social and economic impacts, the World Health Organization declared mpox a public health emergency of international concern on July 23, 2022 (2–3). Mpox is an infectious disease endemic to regions of Central and West Africa. It is caused by the enveloped DNA virus monkeypox virus (MPXV) and is characterized by fever, headache, myalgia, lymphadenopathy, and a vesiculopustular rash that can involve the face, extremities, and genital region (3). Mpox is primarily transmitted through direct contact with active lesions, contaminated materials, bodily fluids, or respiratory transmission at close range (4,5). Mpox infections are categorized into 2 genetically distinct clades, clade I and clade II. Clade II infections, which were responsible for the global outbreak that began in 2022, are generally associated with less severe disease and reduced transmissibility (5). Historically, clade I mpox infections have demonstrated greater virulence, mortality, and transmission (6). The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) National Wastewater Surveillance System initiated wastewater testing for MPXV in October 2022, five months after the mpox outbreak began in the United States. For underreported and stigmatized infections such as mpox, traditional case-based surveillance can present challenges, including incomplete capture of subclinical or unreported cases, making wastewater surveillance a valuable complementary approach to clinical mpox surveillance (5,6). Early work demonstrated that viral shedding through urine, feces, respiratory secretions, and skin lesions can result in detectable MPXV in wastewater, supporting wastewater-based epidemiology as a viable approach for monitoring and quantifying community transmission (2,7,8). In 1 study, MPXV detections in wastewater were shown to precede the identification of the clinical cases, highlighting its potential for early outbreak detection (9). Another study reported increases in wastewater viral concentrations ahead of reported clinical cases (5). Studies have also documented correlations between wastewater MPXV concentrations and incident mpox cases within corresponding sewersheds, supporting the utility of wastewater surveillance as a proxy for community-level transmission (10). Finally, wastewater detections in areas without corresponding clinical reports may help identify communities where mpox transmission might otherwise remain undetected because of social stigma, limited clinical recognition, or constrained diagnostic capacity (5,9). Recognizing wastewater surveillance as a valuable strategy for early identification of infectious disease activity, the North Carolina Department of Health and Human Services (NCDHHS) integrated mpox monitoring into its statewide wastewater surveillance program. In September 2023, nonvariola orthopoxvirus testing was implemented at selected wastewater surveillance sites across the state. That assay detects orthopoxviruses including vaccinia, cowpox, and all clades of MPXV. Primary sites were facilities in Asheville, Charlotte, Greensboro, Greenville, and Raleigh; additional periodic testing was conducted at selected sites in Cary, Chapel Hill, North Durham, and South Durham. To evaluate mpox wastewater surveillance program in North Carolina, we conducted this study to estimate sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV) relative to confirmed clinical cases. Study Area and Surveillance Period We conducted a retrospective diagnostic performance analysis to evaluate wastewater surveillance for detecting MPXV circulation in North Carolina. For the period October 29, 2023–May 31, 2025, we compared wastewater detections from the North Carolina Wastewater Monitoring Network, operated by the NCDHHS, with confirmed clinical mpox cases using a +17-day temporal window. We assumed clinical case reporting to be complete for the purposes of this analysis. The study included data from 16 publicly owned wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) with defined catchment areas serving a combined population of 2,002,864 persons (Table 1). Facilities were in urban and semiurban regions and consisted of 4 plants in Charlotte, 3 plants each in Cary and Raleigh, and 1 plant each in Asheville, Chapel Hill, Greensboro, Greenville, North Durham, and South Durham. During the study period, 45 confirmed mpox cases occurred within the included sewersheds. We excluded sites sampled through CDC-contracted programs (Verily, https://verily.com) and WastewaterSCAN (https://www.wastewaterscan.org) because of differences in laboratory methods, assays, reporting structures, and sampling frequency. Clinical Case Data We also obtained clinical case data from NCDHHS. A confirmed mpox case was defined according to the Council of State and Territorial Epidemiologists case definition from 2022 (22-ID-10) as detection of nonvariola orthopoxvirus or MPXV DNA in a clinical specimen by PCR in a patient with compatible symptoms (11). We defined case date as date of symptom onset. We geocoded cases using residential address and spatially assigned them to sewersheds by using ArcGIS Pro (Esri, https://www.esri.com). Wastewater Sample Collection and Laboratory Testing. Influent wastewater was collected as 24-hour composite samples approximately 1 time/week at each WWTP except for the 3 plants in Cary and those in Chapel Hill, North Durham, and South Durham, which were only sampled selectively over the study period, generally in response to concerns about a confirmed or suspected mpox case in the general area. Samples were transported on ice and processed within 24 hours at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. We quantified MPXV DNA using the CDC Non-variola Orthopoxvirus Generic Real-Time PCR Test (12). We originally optimized the assay in a wastewater matrix by conducting a thermal gradient from 62°C–52°C to see which annealing temperature resulted in the greatest separation from positive and negative droplet clusters (Appendix Figure). analysis.research_question_and_background: Since the first mpox case in a nonendemic region, mpox has become an increasing public health concern in the United States, prompting the need for improved surveillance methods beyond clinical case reporting.
analysis.study_design_and_population: During October 29, 2023–May 2025, 801 wastewater samples were collected from 16 treatment plants serving approximately 2 million residents in North Carolina, USA.
analysis.methods: Wastewater samples were analyzed using the CDC Non-variola Orthopoxvirus Generic Real-Time PCR Test, with viral gene copies normalized to flow rate and population within the sewershed. The assay limit of detection was theoretically estimated at 500 copies/L, and a +17-day alignment window was used to assess temporal concordance with reported clinical cases.
analysis.main_results: The overall sensitivity of wastewater detection for identifying temporally aligned reported mpox cases was 10.6% (95% CI 6.5%–16.7%), increasing to 1.4% (95% CI 0.4%–5.0%) when restricted to detections above the limit of detection. Specificity was high (95.1% to 97.7%), and negative predictive value was approximately 83%.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The study demonstrates that wastewater surveillance provides complementary public health awareness despite low sensitivity, as wastewater detections without temporally aligned cases may reflect unrecognized infections rather than false positives.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: Wastewater surveillance can complement clinical case reporting for mpox by providing high specificity and negative predictive value, particularly in low-incidence settings, though sensitivity remains limited for early warning.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study’s reliance on reported clinical cases as an imperfect reference standard limits diagnostic accuracy estimation, and restricting to detections above the limit of detection markedly reduces sensitivity, potentially compromising early warning capacity.

analysis.summary_en: This study evaluated monkeypox virus (MPXV) surveillance in wastewater across 16 treatment plants in North Carolina, USA, from October 2023 to May 2025, analyzing 801 samples. Using the CDC Non-variola Orthopoxvirus Generic Real-Time PCR Test, viral gene copies were quantified and normalized to flow rate and population. The assay’s theoretical limit of detection was 500 copies/L, and a +17-day alignment window assessed temporal concordance with 45 reported clinical cases. Wastewater detection showed low sensitivity (10.6% overall; 1.4% above LOD) but high specificity (>95%) and moderate negative predictive value (~83%). Sensitivity increased when trace detections were included, suggesting low-level signals contribute to temporal alignment. The authors conclude that wastewater surveillance complements clinical reporting by providing high specificity and negative predictive value, though sensitivity remains limited for early warning.

papers.title: Drivers of Viral Spillover: An Examination of How Pathogens Spread
papers.abstract: The occurrence of viral zoonotic spillover (the transmission of viruses from animals to humans) has attracted worldwide attention due to mounting concerns regarding viral threats such as avian influenza, Hendra, monkeypox, Nipah and bat coronaviruses. It is evident that these events deviate significantly from natural occurrences, being the conflation of ecological, environmental and social factors that are profoundly altering the boundaries between the animal and human domains. Consequently, in order to comprehend both the contemporary and prospective drivers of zoonotic viral spillover, a coordinated, comprehensive global One Health response is essential. The purpose of the present review is to analyze prevailing pathways of transmission between animal reservoirs and human populations. This examination involves the analysis of historical cases, including those of SARS and Ebola, as well as recent occurrences, such as the global pandemic of SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19). A secondary objective of this review is to comprehend the fundamental mechanisms of cross-species transmission. The development of effective strategies to mitigate the emergence of zoonotic viruses and prevent future pandemics is contingent on a robust understanding of these mechanisms. This analysis is key to identifying pandemic pathogens and preventing the spread of zoonotic viruses. In conclusion, the review provides a thorough evaluation of current global strategies to prevent the spread of zoonotic viruses, highlighting gaps in our understanding and areas for further research.

papers.abstract_zh: 由于人们对禽流感、亨德拉病毒、猴痘、尼帕病毒和蝙蝠冠状病毒等病毒威胁的日益担忧,人畜共患病毒 跨物种溢出(从动物传染给人类的病毒 传播)的出现引起了全世界的关注。显然,这些事件与自然发生的事件有很大的偏差,它们是生态、环境和社会因素的综合体,深刻地改变了动物和人类领域之间的界限。因此,为了了解人畜共患病毒 跨物种溢出 的当代和未来驱动因素,协调一致、全面的全球“同一个健康”应对措施至关重要。本综述的目的是分析动物 储存宿主 和人类之间 传播 的普遍通路。这项检查涉及对历史病例的分析,包括 SARS 和埃博拉病毒的病例,以及最近发生的事件,例如 SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) 的全球大流行。本次综述的第二个目标是理解跨物种 传播 的基本机制。制定有效策略来减少人畜共患病毒的出现并预防未来的流行病取决于对这些机制的深入了解。该分析对于识别大流行病原体和防止人畜共患病毒传播至关重要。总之,该审查对当前防止人畜共患病毒传播的全球战略进行了全面评估,突显了我们理解上的差距和需要进一步研究的领域。

papers.title: Infections and sepsis
papers.abstract: Abstract This chapter provides an up-to-date overview of infection screening, management, and prevention in pregnancy, with a particular focus on sepsis. It covers national guidance on antenatal screening for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and rubella, emphasising the importance of early detection and multidisciplinary care to reduce vertical transmission and improve outcomes. The chapter details the significance of group B haemolytic Streptococcus, outlining risk factors, screening protocols, and recommendations for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Common infections such as influenza, urinary tract infections, chickenpox, toxoplasmosis, Mpox, and COVID-19 are discussed, with practical midwifery advice for diagnosis, treatment options, and prevention. The chapter highlights the increased risk of sepsis in pregnancy due to immunological changes and obstetric interventions, stressing the need for prompt recognition, rapid intervention, and multidisciplinary collaboration. Key clinical signs, assessment tools, and the Sepsis Six protocol are presented to support early identification and management. Throughout, the chapter integrates current research, national standards, and real-world practice, equipping midwives to deliver safe, effective care and reduce maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality associated with infections and sepsis.

source_records.abstract: Abstract This chapter provides an up-to-date overview of infection screening, management, and prevention in pregnancy, with a particular focus on sepsis. It covers national guidance on antenatal screening for syphilis, HIV, hepatitis B, and rubella, emphasising the importance of early detection and multidisciplinary care to reduce vertical transmission and improve outcomes. The chapter details the significance of group B haemolytic Streptococcus, outlining risk factors, screening protocols, and recommendations for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis. Common infections such as influenza, urinary tract infections, chickenpox, toxoplasmosis, Mpox, and COVID-19 are discussed, with practical midwifery advice for diagnosis, treatment options, and prevention. The chapter highlights the increased risk of sepsis in pregnancy due to immunological changes and obstetric interventions, stressing the need for prompt recognition, rapid intervention, and multidisciplinary collaboration. Key clinical signs, assessment tools, and the Sepsis Six protocol are presented to support early identification and management. Throughout, the chapter integrates current research, national standards, and real-world practice, equipping midwives to deliver safe, effective care and reduce maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality associated with infections and sepsis.

papers.abstract_zh: 摘要 本章提供了妊娠期感染筛查、管理和预防的最新概述,特别关注败血症。它涵盖了梅毒、艾滋病毒、乙型肝炎和风疹产前筛查的国家指南,强调早期检测和多学科护理对于减少垂直 传播 和改善结果的重要性。本章详细介绍了 B 族溶血性链球菌的重要性,概述了危险因素、筛查方案以及产时抗生素预防的建议。讨论了流感、尿路感染、水痘、弓形体病、猴痘 和 COVID-19 等常见感染,并提供了有关 诊断、治疗 选项和预防的实用助产建议。本章强调了由于免疫变化和产科干预导致妊娠期脓毒症风险增加,强调需要及时识别、快速干预和多学科合作。提出了关键的临床症状、评估工具和脓毒症六号方案以支持早期识别和管理。本章自始至终整合了当前的研究、国家标准和现实世界的实践,使助产士能够提供安全、有效的护理,并降低孕产妇和新生儿的发病率以及与感染和败血症相关的 死亡率。

papers.full_text: Lorsque des cas suspects de mpox, de fièvres hémorragiques virales, de rage et d’autres maladies virales apparaissent au Cameroun, des échantillons parviennent à mon laboratoire au Centre Pasteur du Cameroun, à Yaoundé. Je les analyse et je transmets les résultats au ministère de la Santé publique. Mais mon travail ne s’arrête pas au diagnostic. Je veux comprendre d’où viennent les virus, comment ils se propagent et pourquoi certains restent cachés. Au départ, je voulais devenir médecin, inspirée par ma mère, qui était infirmière. Mais comme l’université la plus proche ne disposait pas de faculté de médecine, j’ai étudié l’analyse médicale à la place. Au cours de mes stages à l’hôpital, j’ai été fascinée par les organismes à l’origine des maladies et j’ai réalisé que je voulais comprendre les infections. Après avoir obtenu ma licence, j’ai poursuivi un master professionnel à Yaoundé. Au cours de la deuxième année, j’ai été sélectionnée pour intégrer un programme régional de master de recherche très sélectif au Gabon. J’ai mené à bien ces deux cursus tout en poursuivant mes travaux de recherche, puis j’ai décroché mon premier stage de recherche en France, ce qui a renforcé mon intérêt pour la virologie. Ma thèse de doctorat portait sur le virus T-lymphotrope humain de type 1 (HTLV-1), un rétrovirus humain dont on connaît encore beaucoup moins les mécanismes d’action que ceux du VIH. Au cours de mes recherches doctorales au Gabon, j’ai travaillé avec des communautés forestières, prélevant des échantillons auprès de plus de 2 000 personnes. Cette expérience a façonné ma vision « One Health ». J’ai pris conscience que les virus sont liés aux environnements dans lesquels ils circulent, et que la santé humaine, animale et celle des écosystèmes doivent être considérées conjointement lors de l’étude des maladies. Après avoir obtenu mon doctorat en 2018, je suis retournée au Cameroun et j’ai ensuite rejoint le Centre Pasteur du Cameroun en tant que chercheuse en 2022. Je dirige aujourd’hui le laboratoire national de référence pour la variole du singe, les fièvres hémorragiques virales et la rage. Mon travail en santé publique détermine souvent mes questions de recherche. Lorsque j’ai commencé à étudier la variole du singe, le Cameroun disposait de peu d’informations génomiques. J’ai analysé les cas signalés de 1979 à 2022 afin de réaliser la première étude exhaustive sur la variole du singe dans le pays.1 J’, je souhaitais montrer que les scientifiques camerounais étaient capables de mener des recherches de grande envergure ; c’est pourquoi la publication ne comprenait que des auteurs camerounais. L’étude a révélé que le Cameroun présente une particularité : les deux principaux clades de la variole du singe y circulent. Nous avons constaté que le fleuve Sanaga semblait marquer la limite de leur répartition, les différentes lignées virales étant associées à des écosystèmes forestiers distincts. Ces résultats ont soulevé des questions sur la manière dont le virus circule et sur la possibilité que des environnements différents abritent des réservoirs animaux différents. La mise en place d’un programme national de recherche sur la variole du singe a nécessité le développement des outils et de l’expertise nécessaires pour enquêter localement sur les épidémies. Lorsque j’ai commencé à travailler sur la variole du singe, le Cameroun disposait de capacités génomiques limitées et dépendait souvent de laboratoires extérieurs pour les analyses. Mettre en place ces capacités n’a pas été facile. Comme de nombreux scientifiques travaillant dans des contextes aux ressources limitées, j’ai souvent mené mes recherches sans financement dédié. De nombreuses demandes de subventions ont été rejetées, mais j’ai continué à développer des questions de recherche grâce à des collaborations, aux ressources de laboratoire disponibles et aux possibilités de formation. J’ai impliqué des étudiants dans des projets, sollicité le soutien de réseaux scientifiques et poursuivi le prélèvement d’échantillons tout en recherchant des financements. J’ai appris le séquençage de nouvelle génération lors d’un atelier régional au Nigeria et j’ai œuvré à la mise en place de cette technologie au niveau local. J’ai ensuite été l’un des pionniers du séquençage complet du génome de la variole du singe au Centre Pasteur du Cameroun, ce qui a permis au Cameroun d’analyser les virus localement plutôt que de dépendre entièrement de laboratoires extérieurs.2 Je continue à m’attaquer aux questions restées sans réponse. Mes recherches sur le HTLV-1 visent à déterminer si le virus circule parmi les donneurs de sang au Cameroun. Dans le cadre de ces travaux, j’ai collecté plus de 3 000 échantillons. Un autre mystère continue de me tenir en haleine. En 2023, deux enfants sont décédés après avoir développé de graves symptômes hémorragiques. Les tests de dépistage des virus connus se sont révélés négatifs, mais des investigations plus approfondies ont montré la présence d’un agent infectieux. Les échantillons ont provoqué la paralysie puis la mort de souris nouveau-nées, ce qui a donné lieu à des travaux de séquençage. Malgré une collaboration internationale, l’agent pathogène n’a toujours pas été identifié. La recherche scientifique au Cameroun reste difficile en raison d’un financement limité, de problèmes d’équipement et d’un manque d’expertise spécialisée. Mais je pense que les collaborations ne doivent pas se limiter à l’envoi d’échantillons à l’étranger ; elles doivent permettre le transfert de connaissances, de technologies et de compétences. Je suis rentré chez moi parce que je voulais créer l’environnement scientifique dont j’aurais rêvé à mes débuts, un environnement où les scientifiques africains peuvent mener des découvertes qui protègent leurs communautés et apportent des solutions à l’échelle mondiale. Ma devise est simple : la science en Afrique, pour l’Afrique, par les Africains et pour le monde.

J’ai analysé les cas signalés de 1979 à 2022 afin de réaliser la première étude exhaustive sur la variole du singe dans le pays.1 J’, je souhaitais montrer que les scientifiques camerounais étaient capables de mener des recherches de grande envergure ; c’est pourquoi la publication ne comprenait que des auteurs camerounais. L’étude a révélé que le Cameroun présente une particularité : les deux principaux clades de la variole du singe y circulent. Nous avons constaté que le fleuve Sanaga semblait marquer la limite de leur répartition, les différentes lignées virales étant associées à des écosystèmes forestiers distincts. Ces résultats ont soulevé des questions sur la manière dont le virus circule et sur la possibilité que des environnements différents abritent des réservoirs animaux différents. La mise en place d’un programme national de recherche sur la variole du singe a nécessité le développement des outils et de l’expertise nécessaires pour enquêter localement sur les épidémies. Lorsque j’ai commencé à travailler sur la variole du singe, le Cameroun disposait de capacités génomiques limitées et dépendait souvent de laboratoires extérieurs pour les analyses. Mettre en place ces capacités n’a pas été facile. Comme de nombreux scientifiques travaillant dans des contextes aux ressources limitées, j’ai souvent mené mes recherches sans financement dédié. De nombreuses demandes de subventions ont été rejetées, mais j’ai continué à développer des questions de recherche grâce à des collaborations, aux ressources de laboratoire disponibles et aux possibilités de formation. J’ai impliqué des étudiants dans des projets, sollicité le soutien de réseaux scientifiques et poursuivi le prélèvement d’échantillons tout en recherchant des financements. J’ai appris le séquençage de nouvelle génération lors d’un atelier régional au Nigeria et j’ai œuvré à la mise en place de cette technologie au niveau local. J’ai ensuite été l’un des pionniers du séquençage complet du génome de la variole du singe au Centre Pasteur du Cameroun, ce qui a permis au Cameroun d’analyser les virus localement plutôt que de dépendre entièrement de laboratoires extérieurs.2 Je continue à m’attaquer aux questions restées sans réponse. Mes recherches sur le HTLV-1 visent à déterminer si le virus circule parmi les donneurs de sang au Cameroun. Dans le cadre de ces travaux, j’ai collecté plus de 3 000 échantillons. Un autre mystère continue de me tenir en haleine. En 2023, deux enfants sont décédés après avoir développé de graves symptômes hémorragiques. Les tests de dépistage des virus connus se sont révélés négatifs, mais des investigations plus approfondies ont montré la présence d’un agent infectieux. Les échantillons ont provoqué la paralysie puis la mort de souris nouveau-nées, ce qui a donné lieu à des travaux de séquençage. Malgré une collaboration internationale, l’agent pathogène n’a toujours pas été identifié. La recherche scientifique au Cameroun reste difficile en raison d’un financement limité, de problèmes d’équipement et d’un manque d’expertise spécialisée. Mais je pense que les collaborations ne doivent pas se limiter à l’envoi d’échantillons à l’étranger ; elles doivent permettre le transfert de connaissances, de technologies et de compétences. Je suis rentré chez moi parce que je voulais créer l’environnement scientifique dont j’aurais rêvé à mes débuts, un environnement où les scientifiques africains peuvent mener des découvertes qui protègent leurs communautés et apportent des solutions à l’échelle mondiale. Ma devise est simple : la science en Afrique, pour l’Afrique, par les Africains et pour le monde.

papers.full_text_excerpt: Lorsque des cas suspects de mpox, de fièvres hémorragiques virales, de rage et d’autres maladies virales apparaissent au Cameroun, des échantillons parviennent à mon laboratoire au Centre Pasteur du Cameroun, à Yaoundé. Je les analyse et je transmets les résultats au ministère de la Santé publique. Mais mon travail ne s’arrête pas au diagnostic. Je veux comprendre d’où viennent les virus, comment ils se propagent et pourquoi certains restent cachés. Au départ, je voulais devenir médecin, inspirée par ma mère, qui était infirmière. Mais comme l’université la plus proche ne disposait pas de faculté de médecine, j’ai étudié l’analyse médicale à la place. Au cours de mes stages à l’hôpital, j’ai été fascinée par les organismes à l’origine des maladies et j’ai réalisé que je voulais comprendre les infections. Après avoir obtenu ma licence, j’ai poursuivi un master professionnel à Yaoundé. Au cours de la deuxième année, j’ai été sélectionnée pour intégrer un programme régional de master de recherche très sélectif au Gabon. J’ai mené à bien ces deux cursus tout en poursuivant mes travaux de recherche, puis j’ai décroché mon premier stage de recherche en France, ce qui a renforcé mon intérêt pour la virologie. Ma thèse de doctorat portait sur le virus T-lymphotrope humain de type 1 (HTLV-1), un rétrovirus humain dont on connaît encore beaucoup moins les mécanismes d’action que ceux du VIH. Au cours de mes recherches doctorales au Gabon, j’ai travaillé avec des communautés forestières, prélevant des échantillons auprès de plus de 2 000 personnes. Cette expérience a façonné ma vision « One Health ». J’ai pris conscience que les virus sont liés aux environnements dans lesquels ils circulent, et que la santé humaine, animale et celle des écosystèmes doivent être considérées conjoi…

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to understand the origins, transmission and persistence of the mpox virus, particularly in the context of limited genomic data and the need for local research capacity in Cameroon.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The research involved analyzing reported cases of mpox from 1979 to 2022, with a focus on the national reference laboratory for mpox, viral hemorrhagic fevers and rabies at the Centre Pasteur du Cameroun in Yaoundé, and included over 2,000 samples from forest communities.
analysis.methods: The study utilized genomic sequencing techniques, including next-generation sequencing, and involved collaboration with international networks to analyze samples and develop local research capabilities.
analysis.main_results: The study found that both main clades of the mpox virus circulate in Cameroon, with the Sanaga River acting as a boundary between their distribution, and different viral lineages associated with distinct forest ecosystems.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest that the virus may be linked to different animal reservoirs in specific environments, raising questions about its transmission dynamics and the need for integrated One Health approaches.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results inform surveillance strategies by highlighting the importance of understanding local viral ecology and the necessity of developing regional diagnostic and research capacities to address mpox outbreaks effectively.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by the lack of dedicated funding and the reliance on international collaboration, but the evidence is strong due to the comprehensive genomic analysis and local context.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the origins, transmission and persistence of the mpox virus in Cameroon, emphasizing the need for local research capacity. The research analyzed mpox cases from 1979 to 2022, revealing that both main clades circulate in the country, with the Sanaga River marking their distribution boundary. The findings suggest that different viral lineages may be associated with distinct forest ecosystems, potentially indicating separate animal reservoirs. This highlights the importance of a One Health approach for understanding and managing mpox. The study underscores the challenges of limited funding and international reliance, but the genomic analysis provides strong evidence for local insights. The results have significant implications for surveillance and public health strategies in Cameroon and beyond, emphasizing the need for regional research capabilities to address viral diseases effectively.

papers.abstract_zh: 在喀麦隆出现疑似猴痘、病毒性出血热、狂犬病及其他病毒性疾病的疑似病例时,样本会被送至我在雅温得的喀麦隆巴斯德中心实验室。我对这些样本进行分析,并将结果传递给公共卫生部。但我的工作并不止于诊断。我希望了解病毒的来源、传播方式以及为何某些病毒仍隐藏不露。最初,我受母亲——一位护士的影响,立志成为医生。但由于最近的大学未设医学院,我转而攻读医学分析专业。在医院实习期间,我被致病微生物深深吸引,并意识到自己想要研究感染。获得学士学位后,我在雅温得继续攻读专业硕士。第二年,我被选中进入加蓬一个极具竞争性的区域研究型硕士项目。在完成这两个学业的同时,我继续开展研究工作,随后在法国获得了首个研究实习机会,这进一步增强了我对病毒学的兴趣。我的博士论文研究了人类T淋巴细胞趋化性病毒1型(HTLV-1),一种人类反转录病毒,其作用机制的研究程度远不及艾滋病病毒(HIV)。在加蓬攻读博士期间,我与森林社区合作,从2000多人身上采集样本。这一经历塑造了我的「One Health」(同一健康)理念。我意识到,病毒与其流行环境密切相关,人类、动物及生态系统的健康必须被视为一个整体。

What to know There are two types of the virus that causes monkeypox, clade I and clade II. Both types can be spread, treated, and prevented in the same ways. Each clade has two subclades (clade Ia and clade Ib; clade IIa and IIb). Recent outbreaks of monkeypox have spread initially through intimate or sexual contact. In some cases, monkeypox was then spread within households. Recent travel-associated clade I monkeypox cases have almost exclusively been attributed to subclade Ib; there have been no deaths associated with these cases and most people had relatively mild illness. The ongoing global outbreak of clade IIb monkeypox that began in 2022 has caused more than 100,000 cases in 122 total countries, including 115 countries where monkeypox was not previously reported. CDC has vaccination recommendations for people at risk in the United States or who are traveling to countries with clade I outbreaks or new clade II outbreaks. Current situation In the United States Clade I monkeypox The risk posed by the clade I monkeypox outbreak to most people within the United States remains low. Since November 2024, there have been more than 50 laboratory-confirmed cases of clade I monkeypox in the United States. More than half were diagnosed in people who: Had recently traveled from areas associated with the outbreak in Central and Eastern Africa; Had recently traveled from parts of Western Europe where newer outbreaks are being reported; OR Were linked to people who had traveled from these areas. We expect additional cases in Europe and the United States. Reminder Vaccination is an important tool in stopping the spread of monkeypox. If you have certain risk factors that make you eligible, you can help protect yourself from monkeypox by getting the 2-dose monkeypox vaccine. Monkeypox Vaccination Clade II monkeypox Clade II monkeypox is still circulating at low levels. Fall 2025 marked the highest monthly case counts since the peak of the outbreak in 2022. Clade I Monkeypox Outbreaks Cases of clade I monkeypox have been diagnosed worldwide. Clade II Monkeypox Outbreaks Clade II monkeypox is spreading in the United States and around the world. Across the globe Clade I monkeypox Outbreaks of clade I monkeypox in Central and Eastern Africa continue. Beginning in Fall 2025, several countries in Western Europe began reporting clade Ib monkeypox cases among individuals who had no documented history of international travel. These cases were likely related to male-to-male sexual contact. Other travel-associated cases of clade I monkeypox have been reported from other parts of Africa, as well as Asia, Europe, the Middle East, North America, South America, and Australia. Recent monkeypox outbreaks have low death rates During recent outbreaks, death rates ranged from than less than 0.5% (clade Ib) to about 3% (clade Ia). Clade II is the type that caused the ongoing global outbreak that began in 2022. Fewer than 0.1% of people infected with clade II die from the disease. Clade II monkeypox For global case data for clade I and clade II monkeypox since January 1, 2024, see Global Mpox Trends. Confirmed cases include those that are laboratory confirmed as monkeypox virus and may include cases only confirmed as orthopoxvirus. These data are provided for situational awareness and are subject to change. What CDC is doing CDC raises awareness for U.S. healthcare providers, including the latest guidance for diagnosing monkeypox and clinical decision-making. CDC continues critical work to protect the United States from emerging and infectious diseases. CDC has collaborated closely with key partners in affected countries to help support efforts to stop monkeypox at the source. CDC works closely with U.S. state, tribal, local, and territorial public health departments to provide recommendations for clinical management, diagnosis, and prevention of domestic monkeypox cases. in the U.S. CDC continually increases capacity in communities across the United States for early detection of monkeypox through existing surveillance systems, including wastewater testing. CDC raises awareness for healthcare providers, including the latest guidance for diagnosing monkeypox and clinical decision-making. CDC collaborated with governmental and civil society partners in affected countries to collect and analyze case data, and to identify how monkeypox is spreading. CDC coordinated technical assistance in response to urgent in-country needs, including: increasing the number of monkeypox testing sites; improving specimen transport networks to quickly identify new cases; assisting with Ministry of Health-led vaccine implementation; strengthening emergency management systems; improving case surveillance; and training healthcare workers. CDC's staff throughout Africa provide critical, real-time information to inform U.S. preparedness efforts. In the United States CDC works closely with state, tribal, local, and territorial public health departments to provide recommendations for clinical management, diagnosis, and prevention of monkeypox cases in the U.S. CDC continually increases capacity in communities across the United States for early detection of monkeypox through existing surveillance systems, including wastewater testing. CDC raises awareness for healthcare providers, including the latest guidance for diagnosing monkeypox and clinical decision-making. CDC has information and recommendations for members of the public, including travelers: Destinations | Travelers' Health, Travel Health Notices, and Health Alert Network advisories. CDC continues to work with international partners to help reduce monkeypox transmission. analysis.time: The current situation report was published on August 27, 2026. The ongoing global outbreak of clade IIb monkeypox began in 2022, and recent outbreaks have been reported since Fall 2025.
analysis.location_and_population: The report covers the United States and global locations, including Central and Eastern Africa, Western Europe, and other regions such as Asia, the Middle East, North America, South America, and Australia. The affected population includes individuals who have traveled from outbreak areas or been linked to them, particularly those involved in male-to-male sexual contact.
analysis.event: Monkeypox outbreaks are ongoing globally, with clade IIb being the primary type causing the outbreak since 2022. Clade I monkeypox outbreaks have been reported in the United States and other regions, with cases linked to travel or sexual contact. The CDC reports that these outbreaks are being monitored and managed.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The ongoing global outbreak of clade IIb monkeypox has caused more than 100,000 cases in 122 countries, including 115 countries where monkeypox was not previously reported. In the United States, since November 2024, there have been more than 50 laboratory-confirmed cases of clade I monkeypox. The risk posed by clade I monkeypox to most people in the U.S. remains low, and the death rate for clade Ib is less than 0.5%, while for clade Ia it is about 3%.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC is actively raising awareness among healthcare providers, providing guidance for diagnosing monkeypox and clinical decision-making. They are also working with public health departments to increase detection capacity through surveillance systems and wastewater testing. Vaccination recommendations are in place for people at risk, and the CDC collaborates with international partners to reduce transmission.

analysis.brief_en: The CDC's August 27, 2026, report outlines the current situation of monkeypox globally and in the United States. The ongoing global outbreak of clade IIb monkeypox, which began in 2022, has led to over 100,000 cases in 122 countries, including 115 where it was previously unreported. In the U.S., more than 50 laboratory-confirmed cases of clade I monkeypox have been reported since November 2024, primarily linked to travel from Central and Eastern Africa or Western Europe, or through sexual contact. The risk to most people in the U.S. remains low, with clade Ib cases having a death rate of less than 0.5%. The CDC emphasizes vaccination as a key tool for prevention and has provided recommendations for those at risk. They are also enhancing surveillance systems, including wastewater testing, to detect monkeypox early and are collaborating with international partners to manage the outbreak. The report highlights the importance of clinical management and public health measures to control the spread of the virus.

In the U.S., more than 50 laboratory-confirmed cases of clade I monkeypox have been reported since November 2024, primarily linked to travel from Central and Eastern Africa or Western Europe, or through sexual contact. The risk to most people in the U.S. remains low, with clade Ib cases having a death rate of less than 0.5%. The CDC emphasizes vaccination as a key tool for prevention and has provided recommendations for those at risk. They are also enhancing surveillance systems, including wastewater testing, to detect monkeypox early and are collaborating with international partners to manage the outbreak. The report highlights the importance of clinical management and public health measures to control the spread of the virus.

What to know There have been outbreaks of clade I monkeypox in Central and Eastern Africa since late 2023. Since January 2024, more than 55,000 confirmed cases of clade I monkeypox have been reported globally, including more than 150 deaths. Newer outbreaks in several Western European countries are likely related to this ongoing outbreak. Transmission dynamics are changing. Only a small proportion of exported clade I monkeypox cases worldwide this year have originated in Central or Eastern African countries. Recent travel-associated clade I monkeypox cases have almost exclusively been attributed to subclade Ib; there have been no deaths associated with these cases and available data have detailed relatively mild disease courses. Outbreak overview In the United States The risk posed by the clade I monkeypox outbreak to most people within the United States remains low. The risk to men who have sex with men is low to moderate. Clade I cases in the United States have increased in frequency since March 2026. As of July 2026, there have been more than 50 clade I monkeypox cases reported in the United States. More than half of all U.S. cases were diagnosed in people who: Had recently traveled to areas associated with the outbreak in Central and Eastern Africa; Had recently traveled to parts of Western Europe where newer outbreaks are being reported; OR Were linked to people who had traveled from these areas. CDC expects additional cases in Europe and the United States. Preventing Monkeypox While Traveling Learn where monkeypox is spreading and how to lower your risk of getting it during travel. In Central and Eastern Africa Clade Ia monkeypox outbreaks began impacting western areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in 2024. Available data indicate that clade Ia monkeypox has spread through sexual contact, regular household contact, and encounters with infected dead or live wild animals. Clade Ib monkeypox cases initially impacted eastern areas of DRC in late 2023. This subclade has driven much of the spread throughout Central and Eastern Africa and most travel-associated cases to other parts of the world. Available data indicate that these cases at first spread through heterosexual intimate or sexual contact between adults, then spread likely occurred within households, including to children. The disease spread in 2024 and 2025 to neighboring countries of DRC, only some of which are endemic for the virus that causes monkeypox, and sustained local spread occurred. As of April 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo is still the country with the majority of clade Ib cases. Outside Central and Eastern Africa Several countries in other parts of Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, and South America, as well as Australia, have confirmed clade I monkeypox cases mostly in travelers who'd recently been in areas with clade I outbreaks. To date, there have been more than 300 clade Ib cases in high-income countries, and no deaths have been reported. Beginning in Fall 2025, several countries in Western Europe began reporting clade Ib monkeypox cases among individuals who had no documented history of international travel. These cases were likely related to intimate or sexual exposure among men who have sex with men. We expect additional cases in Europe and the United States. For data since January 1, 2024, see 2022-24 Monkeypox (Monkeypox) Outbreak: Global Trends (shinyapps.io). Confirmed cases include those that are laboratory confirmed as monkeypox virus and may include cases only confirmed as orthopoxvirus. These data are provided for situational awareness and are subject to change. Clade I monkeypox and children Early in the Central and Eastern African outbreak, a high proportion of suspected cases in some areas were reported in children younger than 15 years of age. Historically, cases of monkeypox in children where monkeypox occurs regularly often happen after contact with wild animals that carry the disease. People then can spread the disease to close contacts, including in their households. The number of children with suspected monkeypox in this outbreak is probably due to spread within and between close households, the large number of younger people in affected countries, misdiagnosis of other diseases (such as measles), poor sanitary conditions, limited access to health services, and a high level of food insecurity and malnutrition. Based on what we know today, we don't expect to see the same sort of pattern in the United States for several reasons, including smaller household sizes, access to cleaning and disinfecting products, and improved access to medical care, equipment, and information about preventing spread while caring for patients. Notably, there are no consistent reports of schools as drivers of monkeypox transmission during any recent outbreaks. If cases of clade I monkeypox do happen in children the United States, CDC has clinical and public health guidance for reporting, testing, and effective case management. What CDC is doing CDC has been supporting DRC monkeypox research and response for more than 20 years. CDC and other U.S. government agencies have continued working in-country with partners in affected areas on disease surveillance, building local laboratory capacity, strengthening public health and laboratory workforce capacity, case investigation, case management, infection prevention and control, border health, and risk communication and community engagement. CDC staff brought laboratory supplies and trained local staff on laboratory equipment Resources Monkeypox in the United States and Around the World: Current Situation There are outbreaks of clade I and clade II monkeypox around the world. analysis.time: The outbreak of clade I monkeypox began in Central and Eastern Africa since late 2023, with increased frequency in the United States since March 2026. As of July 2026, more than 50 cases were reported in the U.S. and as of April 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) remains the country with the majority of clade Ib cases. The CDC expects additional cases in Europe and the United States.
analysis.location_and_population: The outbreaks have occurred in Central and Eastern Africa, particularly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and have spread to Western European countries and the United States. The affected population includes travelers from outbreak areas, individuals with close contact with infected people, and men who have sex with men in Western Europe.
analysis.event: Outbreaks of clade I monkeypox have been reported in Central and Eastern Africa since late 2023, with newer outbreaks in Western European countries likely related to the ongoing outbreak. The CDC has confirmed that clade I monkeypox cases in the United States have increased since March 2026, and as of July 2026, over 50 cases were reported. These cases are primarily linked to travel or contact with infected individuals.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Since January 2024, more than 55,000 confirmed cases of clade I monkeypox have been reported globally, with over 150 deaths. In the United States, more than 50 cases were reported as of July 2026, and the risk to most people remains low. However, the risk to men who have sex with men is low to moderate. No deaths have been reported in high-income countries for clade Ib cases, and the disease course is relatively mild.

analysis.brief_en: The CDC reports that clade I monkeypox outbreaks have been ongoing in Central and Eastern Africa since late 2023, with more than 55,000 confirmed cases and over 150 deaths globally since January 2024. These outbreaks have spread to Western European countries and the United States, where cases have increased since March 2026. As of July 2026, over 50 clade I monkeypox cases were reported in the U.S., primarily linked to travel or contact with infected individuals. The risk to most people in the U.S. remains low, but it is moderate for men who have sex with men. No deaths have been reported in high-income countries for clade Ib cases, which have been the main driver of the outbreak. The CDC is actively supporting research and response efforts in the DRC and collaborating with partners on disease surveillance, laboratory capacity, and public health measures. The data are subject to change and provided for situational awareness.

analysis.time: Published on 2026-08-25; event onset began on 2026-08-18 with symptom onset and diagnosis confirmed on 2026-08-24.
analysis.location_and_population: Macao Special Administrative Region (SAR), China; resident young adult male.
analysis.event: Macao Health Bureau reported one confirmed imported mpox (monkeypox) case; patient is hospitalized and receiving treatment; case classified as imported based on travel and exposure history.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 1 confirmed case; patient currently stable; no reported deaths; global non-endemic case fatality rate approximately 0.1% since 2022; no secondary cases among household contacts reported.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Health Bureau conducting epidemiological investigation; patient’s household contacts to receive mpox vaccination as prevention; high-risk individuals in Macao can receive pre-exposure prophylaxis via local health centers since 2023-09-14; general public risk assessed as low; guidance issued on safe sexual practices and avoidance of contact with suspected cases or contaminated items.

analysis.brief_en: Macao’s Health Bureau confirmed its first imported mpox case on 25 August 2026 in a young male resident who developed fever, headache and rash after travel. The patient, who had not been vaccinated, was diagnosed on 24 August and is hospitalized in stable condition. Epidemiological investigation indicates likely acquisition abroad through high-risk sexual contact; no local transmission or animal exposure was reported. Contacts will receive preventive vaccination, while Macao continues targeted pre-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk groups since September 2023. Authorities emphasize that mpox risk for the general population remains low and reiterate safe-sex and hygiene measures.

Authorities emphasize that mpox risk for the general population remains low and reiterate safe-sex and hygiene measures.

Photograph: Tchandrou Nitanga/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A man infected with mpox at a hospital in Burundi. Photograph: Tchandrou Nitanga/AFP/Getty Images Mpox is back – and in new countries. How can this outbreak be contained? The public health emergencies in 2022 and 2024 saw the virus reported in 145 countries, but in the new cases children appear particularly affected A fresh outbreak of mpox in Guinea Bissau – the country’s first – means the virus formerly known as monkey pox is back in the headlines. So what has changed? Since 2022, there have been almost 190,000 lab-confirmed cases of mpox reported worldwide in 145 countries. Before then, outbreaks of mpox tended to be relatively small and in a handful of African countries, where the viral infection was known to be endemic. What is mpox? Mpox is an infectious disease that typically starts with flu-like symptoms, including fever, chills and aching muscles. These are followed by a distinctive rash, beginning as raised spots that turn into blisters filled with fluid before forming scabs. View image in fullscreen A colourised electron microscope image shows Mpox virus particles, represented in green, found within infected cultured cells, represented in blue. The virus particles are in various stages of maturity, which accounts for their differences in shape. Photograph: AP It used to be called monkeypox, because the virus was first discovered in captive monkeys in 1958. But during an international outbreak in 2022, there were concerns that the name was fuelling racist and stigmatising language on and offline, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to recommend changing it to mpox. It is endemic to many parts of Africa, with outbreaks historically starting when people ate meat from infected wild animals. But in recent years it has spread beyond the usual areas, with sustained chains of human-to-human transmission. The Atlanta-based Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said this month that mpox was on course to become endemic in the US. Why is it spreading to new countries? There are, broadly, two types of mpox, known as “clades”. Clade I was once called the “Congo Basin clade” and clade II the “West African clade”. The latter sparked a major global outbreak in 2022 when it appeared to undergo some changes that allowed it to spread more efficiently from person to person. It is passed on via close contact – in that outbreak, mostly by sexual contact, with men who have sex with men at the highest risk. View image in fullscreen A Red Cross worker disinfects a tent in the Don Bosco camps for internally displaced people in Goma, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Photograph: Moise Kasereka/EPA In June 2024, researchers raised the alarm about a new variant of clade I in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), which also appeared to be spreading more easily between people. That grew into another major international outbreak, which was declared a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO on 14 August 2024. “Emergence of mpox in more countries in west Africa is to be expected,” said Prof Michael Marks, of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine and University College London hospital. “Mpox outbreaks have now been declared in a number of countries in the region, including Guinea and Sierra Leone within the last 12 months. “Mpox spreads by close physical contact. This makes it suitable to spread in a variety of different contexts, such as in close sexual networks, as was seen during the 2022 global pandemic, or areas where many people are living closely together such as settings with refugees and internally displaced people, as was seen in the DRC outbreak over the last few years,” Marks said. What happened to those two big outbreaks? The 2022 outbreak was declared a public health emergency in July that year. After contact-tracing and mass vaccination programmes, the status was lifted in May 2023. There had been about 90,000 infections. View image in fullscreen A passenger passes mpox alerts at Chennai airport in India. Photograph: R Satish Babu/AFP The 2024 outbreak had its international public health emergency status lifted in September 2025, not because the disease had disappeared but because numbers of cases and deaths were declining and officials felt the situation had become better controlled. If genetic testing reveales a new variant, or surveillance suggested an outbreak was spreading particularly fast, making people particularly sick or proving more deadly, global health authorities would be likely to step in again. How worrying is the new outbreak? Cases had not been reported in Guinea Bissau before this outbreak. Unicef said it was concerned that of 46 suspected cases, 23 were children aged under 15 and most of those were aged under four. “The concern about children is that they are at the highest risk of severe disease and death from mpox,” said Dr Aula Abbara, a senior lecturer at Imperial College London and adviser to Médecins Sans Frontières UK. “Young children can become much sicker than healthy adults.” View image in fullscreen Furaha Elisabeth applies medication to the skin of her child, Sagesse Hakizimana, at a health centre near Goma, in the DRC. Photograph: Arlette Bashizi/Reuters However, she cautioned that the apparent over-representation of children in the outbreak data should be interpreted carefully. She said: “There may also be some bias in the data. Families are often more likely to seek healthcare for a sick child than for an adult, particularly in a resource-constrained setting with a fragile health system, such as Guinea-Bissau.” Marks added: “Children have close physical contact with their parents and with each other, and in settings such as Guinea-Bissau are often living in cramped conditions, which make close physical contact and transmission more likely.” Confirmed cases do not appear linked to each other, which suggests the virus is circulating more widely in the community and there are unidentified cases. Are there vaccines and treatments? The WHO recommends two vaccines, which can be given to people at high risk or offered to people who have been in contact with a known case to prevent further spread. The question is where they are available. Marks said: “The major challenge remains that supplies of vaccines are best in high-income countries but worst in low-income settings, where the need and conditions for mpox transmission are highest.” A new global stockpile is due to be launched within weeks, which should mean vaccines can be deployed more rapidly to quell outbreaks. Officials also hope it will allow manufacturers to plan ahead and produce more of the jabs by providing a clear, concrete demand. View image in fullscreen A young mpox patient receives treatment at the Kavumu hospital in Karanrhada, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Photograph: Michael Lunanga/EPA An antiviral called tecovirimat did not appear any better than a placebo when tested on patients with mpox clade I in the DRC, although the question of whether it might help some immunocompromised patients – such as those living with HIV – remains open. That trial did show, however, that giving patients good, supportive care dramatically improved their chances of survival. While vaccines remained an important tool for outbreak control, basic supportive care could be lifesaving, Abbara said. She added that strengthening surveillance, testing, contact tracing and broader public health measures would be critical to understanding and containing the outbreak. “Vaccines are important, but outbreaks are not controlled by vaccines alone,” she said. “Early detection, contact tracing, supportive care and strong public health surveillance remain absolutely essential.” Explore more on these topics Global health Mpox Guinea-Bissau Infectious diseases World Health Organization Health Microbiology news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Trump says NBC’s Kristen ‌Welker should face ‘punishment’ from FCC The kindness of strangers: My car had been towed and my kids had no shoes, then a man made a wonderful offer Man killed by falling sign at Christian festival named as church pays tribute Headteacher saves 900 children from deadly flash flood in Nepal Devastated by floods and overwhelmed by bodies, Nepalis weep for what remains of their homes Most viewed Most viewed

A microscopic image of Mpox virus for illustrative purposes only. Image by NIAID, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons Taipei, Aug. 26 (CNA) Taiwan's Centers for Disease Control (CDC) on Wednesday reported two new cases of Mpox involving the clade Ib strain, marking the first domestic cases of the variant, which is believed to be more transmissible and more easily spread through close physical or intimate contact. Both patients were men in their 30s who had not been vaccinated and had engaged in high-risk sexual behavior with unspecified partners, according to contact tracing. However, the sources of their infections remain unclear, CDC spokesperson Lin Ming-cheng (林明誠) told reporters. The first patient sought medical attention in late July after developing a fever, as well as rashes and pustules on his abdomen and groin. He tested positive for Mpox after his doctor suspected the disease, Lin said. The second patient sought treatment in early August after developing rashes on his trunk and legs, followed by a fever and muscle soreness. He also tested positive after his doctor suspected Mpox and conducted testing, Lin said. As of Aug. 23, Taiwan had recorded 28 Mpox cases, including 19 domestic and nine imported cases, according to the CDC. The figure was lower than the 48 cases reported in 2024 and 31 in 2025 in the same period. A total of nine cases, including the two newly reported domestic cases, have been identified as the clade Ib strain since Taiwan recorded its first imported case in May 2026. The CDC said global experience shows that people infected with either clade Ib or clade II can develop symptoms including fever, swollen lymph nodes, rashes and blisters. Clade Ib is more easily transmitted within households, while people with weakened immune systems, including children, pregnant women and those with chronic illnesses, are more likely to develop severe symptoms, the agency said. The CDC said many people who have contracted Mpox had engaged in high-risk sexual behavior, while nearly 90 percent had not been vaccinated. Vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent Mpox, including infection with the clade Ib and clade II strains, the agency said. Those eligible for publicly funded vaccines include people who have engaged in high-risk sexual behavior in the past year, people who have been diagnosed with a sexually transmitted disease, and people who have had sexual contact with anyone in either of those categories. news.source_body_en: On August 26, 2026, Taiwan's Centers for Disease Control (CDC) reported two new domestic cases of Mpox involving the clade Ib strain, marking the first such cases in the country. Both patients were men in their 30s who had not been vaccinated and engaged in high-risk sexual behavior with unspecified partners. The first patient sought medical attention in late July after developing a fever, rashes, and pustules on his abdomen and groin, while the second patient did so in early August after experiencing rashes on his trunk and legs, followed by a fever and muscle soreness. The CDC confirmed the cases through testing after doctors suspected Mpox based on symptoms. As of August 23, 2026, Taiwan had recorded 28 Mpox cases, including 19 domestic and nine imported cases. Since the first imported case in May 2026, nine cases have been identified as the clade Ib strain. The CDC highlighted that clade Ib is more easily transmitted within households and that individuals with weakened immune systems, such as children, pregnant women, and those with chronic illnesses, are at higher risk of severe symptoms. The sources of infection for the two patients remain unclear, and the CDC is conducting contact tracing. The agency also emphasized that vaccination is the most effective way to prevent Mpox, including infection with the clade Ib strain, and that many cases involved high-risk sexual behavior and lack of vaccination.

news.content: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages August 1, 2026 - August 30, 2026 GO Home Front Page Thu, Aug 27, 2026 page1 Taiwan confirms two local mpox clade Ib cases PROTECTION: Nearly 90 percent of confirmed mpox cases were unvaccinated, the CDC said, adding that current vaccines are effective against clade Ib By Hou Chia-yu and Sam Garcia / Staff reporter, with staff writer Add TT as Preferred Source Two domestic cases of mpox clade Ib have been confirmed this month, marking the first locally acquired infections of the virus strain, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said yesterday. The patients, both men in their 30s, are in stable condition and had not received an mpox vaccine before developing symptoms, the CDC said. The first man developed a fever late last month, followed by a rash and pustules on the abdomen and groin, CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Ming-cheng (林明誠) said. Centers for Disease Control physician Lin Yung-ching explains mpox symptoms and preventive measures in a news conference at the centers in Taipei on April 21. Photo: Lin Chih-yi, Taipei Times He was diagnosed with mpox after seeking medical care and undergoing testing, Lin said. The other man developed a rash on the torso and legs early this month, followed by fever and muscle aches, and after rashes appeared on multiple parts of his body, he was tested, Lin said. Genetic typing confirmed that they were infected with mpox clade Ib, he added. Mpox is a viral infectious disease primarily spread through close contact, including sexual contact, hugging, kissing or direct skin-to-skin contact, the CDC said. The clade Ib strain has symptoms similar to the more common clade II, including fever, swollen lymph nodes, rashes and blisters, but its rash might be more widespread and the virus might spread more easily within households, Lin said. Young children, pregnant women and people with chronic illnesses are at higher risk of severe disease if infected, he said. Mpox vaccines are effective against clade Ib, while the antiviral drug tecovirimat could be used to treat severe cases, he added. As of Sunday, 28 new mpox cases had been recorded in Taiwan this year, including 19 locally acquired cases and nine imported cases, all involving men aged 20 to 50, the CDC said. Since the first imported mpox clade Ib case was reported in May, nine clade Ib infections have been confirmed, including seven imported and two locally acquired cases, it said. Since mpox was designated a Category 2 communicable disease in 2022, Taiwan has recorded 544 cases, including 500 locally acquired cases and 44 imported cases, CDC data showed. Most people with confirmed mpox had a history of higher-risk sexual activity, and nearly 90 percent were unvaccinated against mpox, the centers said. People who engage in higher-risk sexual activity, particularly those without a steady sexual partner, face a higher risk of infection, it said. The risk to the general population remains low, it added. Vaccination remains the most effective way to prevent infection, Lin said, adding that as of last month, 79,216 people had completed the recommended two doses of the vaccine, while 31,755 people had received only one dose. As two doses provide about 90 percent protection against mpox, compared with 40 to 80 percent protection after one dose, those who are considered at risk should complete the two-dose series as soon as possible, he said. In Taiwan, 318 medical institutions offer government-funded mpox vaccines, the CDC said. People who have engaged in higher-risk sexual activity within the past year, have previously had a sexually transmitted infection or have sexual partners with related risk factors are eligible for the government-funded vaccine, it said. Mpox has an incubation period of up to 21 days, and some people might be infectious one to four days before symptoms appear, the centers said. People who develop rashes, blisters or pustules along with symptoms such as fever, headaches, muscle aches or swollen lymph nodes should wear a mask and seek medical attention, and inform their doctor of any travel, exposure and contact history, it said. Healthy Living Airplane Contact Tracing for Mpox Has Ended, and New CDC Data Show Where Travel Risk Actually Sits Published Aug 24, 2026 10:30 PM EDT By Cole Mercer YASUYOSHI CHIBA | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention published its most complete national picture of mpox in more than a year last Thursday, and the numbers point travelers toward a different set of precautions than many have assumed. The new analysis in the agency's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report counted 5,322 confirmed and probable cases across 2024 and 2025. Detections of travel-associated cases increased between the two years, and genomic and epidemiologic data showed evidence of 21 separate importations of the virus into the country. Further importations were observed in 2026 and are expected to continue. What has changed for anyone boarding a plane is the agency's own posture. The CDC discontinued aircraft contact investigations for all mpox clades and subclades in 2025, a decision explained in a separate April report on aircraft contact tracing that examined what happened when infected passengers flew. That earlier investigation followed 60 aircraft contacts of three men who traveled on five commercial flights while infectious with clade I virus, the strain that has driven international concern since 2024. One contact developed fatigue, body aches, and a skin lesion afterward and tested negative. No secondary cases were identified. The authors concluded that the risk of clade I transmission during commercial air travel "appears to be low," consistent with earlier findings for clade II. The Cabin Was Never Where the Risk Concentrated The reason is mechanical rather than reassuring rhetoric. Mpox spreads mainly through close, sustained physical contact with lesions, scabs, or contaminated bedding and clothing, and most often through sexual contact. The kind of contact that produces secondary cases rarely occurs between strangers seated near each other for a few hours. An earlier and much larger investigation reached the same conclusion for the 2022 outbreak strain, finding no secondary cases among 1,538 people who had contact with 113 infected travelers across 221 flights. That finding led the agency to stop routine clade II aircraft investigations back in February 2023, and the newer clade I analysis extended the same reasoning to the remaining clades. The practical translation for a family planning international travel is that seat assignment is not the variable worth worrying about. Vaccination status, destination, and the nature of contact at that destination are. Importations Are Rising Even as Total Cases Hold Steady The topline national figures are close to flat. There were 2,803 cases in 2024 and 2,519 in 2025. The overwhelming majority were clade II, the strain that has circulated domestically since 2022, with about 97.5 percent of sequenced samples descending from the 2022 outbreak lineage. Underneath that stability, two shifts stand out. Reported cases roughly doubled from 423 during September and October 2024 to 873 during the same two months in 2025, before falling to 448 during November and December and returning to background levels by the end of the year. And clade Ib detections rose from a single travel-related case in 2024 to 10 in 2025. Of those 11 cases, three patients were hospitalized and recovered without antiviral treatment, and no deaths were reported. Federal counts have continued climbing since. The CDC's clade I situation summary reports more than 40 laboratory-confirmed clade I cases in the United States since November 2024, and assesses the risk posed by the clade I outbreak to most people in the country as low. No deaths have been reported among roughly 150 clade Ib cases identified in high-income countries. Local transmission has occurred but has not taken hold. A domestic cluster of three cases in October 2025 was traced back to a travel-associated introduction and did not spread further. Sustained clade Ib transmission continues in several European countries, where about 89 percent of cases have occurred among men who have sex with men. City-level surveillance shows the ongoing background. New York City has recorded 102 positive mpox tests since the start of 2026, including 14 in the month ending August 8, according to figures posted by NYC Health and current as of August 13. Vaccination Status Separated Mild Illness from a Hospital Bed The most consequential finding for individual readers concerns outcomes rather than counts. Among 860 patients with complete records, the odds of hospitalization were 9.73 times as high for unvaccinated patients as for those who completed the two-dose JYNNEOS series, after controlling for age group and HIV status. Patients living with HIV had 2.37 times the odds of hospitalization compared with those without. Unvaccinated people accounted for 76.1 percent of cases where vaccination status was recorded. Overall, 9.5 percent of patients were hospitalized, compared with 2 percent among those known to be vaccinated. Deaths remained rare, with five in 2024 and one in 2025. The CDC's conclusion is that persistent low-level transmission of the 2022 strain suggests "a likely transition toward endemic circulation," and the agency recommends that people at risk of exposure complete both doses. That recommendation now explicitly includes travelers heading to countries with ongoing clade I or clade II transmission. Gaps in the Data That Deserve Attention Both reports carry limitations that the agency states directly, and readers should weigh them. The air travel analysis was small. Sixty contacts across five flights is a small base, and health departments managed to interview only 29 of them. The absence of detected transmission in a small sample is weaker evidence than its absence in a large one, though it points in the same direction as the much larger clade II investigation. The hospitalization finding is also less precise than the headline number suggests. The 9.73 figure has a 95 percent confidence interval ranging from 2.93 to 60.65, which is wide enough that the true effect could be much smaller or much larger. The direction is clear; the magnitude is not. The surveillance report relies on passive reporting, so mild infections that do not prompt a medical visit are not captured, and total infections are likely undercounted. Missing data were substantial, with vaccination status absent for 62 percent of cases and HIV status for 68 percent. Analyzing only complete records can introduce selection bias. For households, the reasonable steps are unchanged and modest. Anyone at elevated risk who has not completed the two-dose series can ask a primary care provider, sexual health clinic, or local health department about JYNNEOS, and travelers to affected regions should raise it before departure. People with mpox are advised to delay travel until their illness has resolved. Anyone who develops an unexplained rash after travel or close contact should contact a clinician promptly, mention the exposure, and avoid close physical contact until evaluated. Rapidly worsening symptoms, difficulty breathing, or severe pain warrant urgent care. The agency's recommendations on treatment and vaccination remain the same regardless of clade. The agency updates its monthly U.S. case data in the first week of every month. Read more NIH Plans to Bar Scientists on Visas from the Award That Launches Independent Labs A Smuggling Prosecution Over Inactivated Mpox Samples Has Scientists Warning About Outbreak Preparedness Africa CDC Says Contact Tracing Is Not Working in Congo Ebola Outbreak as Deaths Pass 1,700 Key Questions Answered Can someone catch mpox from a passenger on their flight? Investigations to date have not identified any such case. Among 60 contacts of three infected clade I travelers on five flights, no secondary cases were found, and a larger clade II investigation of 1,538 contacts also found none. Why did the CDC stop tracing airline contacts? Because repeated investigations found no evidence of onboard transmission. The agency discontinued aircraft contact investigations for all mpox clades and subclades in 2025. Does that mean mpox is not a travel concern? No. Travel-associated introductions are rising, and the agency documented 21 importations across 2024 and 2025. The risk is tied to close contact at the destination rather than to the flight itself. Who faces the greatest risk of severe illness? People who are unvaccinated and people living with HIV. Unvaccinated patients had 9.73 times the odds of hospitalization compared with fully vaccinated patients, though the confidence interval around that estimate is wide. Should travelers get vaccinated before an international trip? The CDC recommends the two-dose JYNNEOS series for people at risk of exposure, including travelers to countries with ongoing clade I or clade II transmission. A clinician or local health department can advise on individual eligibility. What symptoms should prompt a call to a clinician? An unexplained rash or lesions, particularly following travel or close physical contact, along with fever, swollen lymph nodes, body aches, or exhaustion. Mention any recent travel when seeking care. How current are these numbers? The national surveillance figures cover cases through December 31, 2025, and are provisional. The count of more than 40 clade I cases reflects the agency's situation summary page as currently posted.
