Healthy Living Airplane Contact Tracing for Mpox Has Ended, and New CDC Data Show Where Travel Risk Actually Sits Published Aug 24, 2026 10:30 PM EDT By Cole Mercer YASUYOSHI CHIBA | AFP via Getty Images Share on Twitter Share on Facebook Share on Pocket The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention published its most complete national picture of mpox in more than a year last Thursday, and the numbers point travelers toward a different set of precautions than many have assumed. The new analysis in the agency's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report counted 5,322 confirmed and probable cases across 2024 and 2025. Detections of travel-associated cases increased between the two years, and genomic and epidemiologic data showed evidence of 21 separate importations of the virus into the country. Further importations were observed in 2026 and are expected to continue. What has changed for anyone boarding a plane is the agency's own posture. The CDC discontinued aircraft contact investigations for all mpox clades and subclades in 2025, a decision explained in a separate April report on aircraft contact tracing that examined what happened when infected passengers flew. That earlier investigation followed 60 aircraft contacts of three men who traveled on five commercial flights while infectious with clade I virus, the strain that has driven international concern since 2024. One contact developed fatigue, body aches, and a skin lesion afterward and tested negative. No secondary cases were identified. The authors concluded that the risk of clade I transmission during commercial air travel "appears to be low," consistent with earlier findings for clade II. The Cabin Was Never Where the Risk Concentrated The reason is mechanical rather than reassuring rhetoric. Mpox spreads mainly through close, sustained physical contact with lesions, scabs, or contaminated bedding and clothing, and most often through sexual contact. The kind of contact that produces secondary cases rarely occurs between strangers seated near each other for a few hours. An earlier and much larger investigation reached the same conclusion for the 2022 outbreak strain, finding no secondary cases among 1,538 people who had contact with 113 infected travelers across 221 flights. That finding led the agency to stop routine clade II aircraft investigations back in February 2023, and the newer clade I analysis extended the same reasoning to the remaining clades. The practical translation for a family planning international travel is that seat assignment is not the variable worth worrying about. Vaccination status, destination, and the nature of contact at that destination are. Importations Are Rising Even as Total Cases Hold Steady The topline national figures are close to flat. There were 2,803 cases in 2024 and 2,519 in 2025. The overwhelming majority were clade II, the strain that has circulated domestically since 2022, with about 97.5 percent of sequenced samples descending from the 2022 outbreak lineage. Underneath that stability, two shifts stand out. Reported cases roughly doubled from 423 during September and October 2024 to 873 during the same two months in 2025, before falling to 448 during November and December and returning to background levels by the end of the year. And clade Ib detections rose from a single travel-related case in 2024 to 10 in 2025. Of those 11 cases, three patients were hospitalized and recovered without antiviral treatment, and no deaths were reported. Federal counts have continued climbing since. The CDC's clade I situation summary reports more than 40 laboratory-confirmed clade I cases in the United States since November 2024, and assesses the risk posed by the clade I outbreak to most people in the country as low. No deaths have been reported among roughly 150 clade Ib cases identified in high-income countries. Local transmission has occurred but has not taken hold. A domestic cluster of three cases in October 2025 was traced back to a travel-associated introduction and did not spread further. Sustained clade Ib transmission continues in several European countries, where about 89 percent of cases have occurred among men who have sex with men. City-level surveillance shows the ongoing background. New York City has recorded 102 positive mpox tests since the start of 2026, including 14 in the month ending August 8, according to figures posted by NYC Health and current as of August 13. Vaccination Status Separated Mild Illness from a Hospital Bed The most consequential finding for individual readers concerns outcomes rather than counts. Among 860 patients with complete records, the odds of hospitalization were 9.73 times as high for unvaccinated patients as for those who completed the two-dose JYNNEOS series, after controlling for age group and HIV status. Patients living with HIV had 2.37 times the odds of hospitalization compared with those without. Unvaccinated people accounted for 76.1 percent of cases where vaccination status was recorded. Overall, 9.5 percent of patients were hospitalized, compared with 2 percent among those known to be vaccinated. Deaths remained rare, with five in 2024 and one in 2025. The CDC's conclusion is that persistent low-level transmission of the 2022 strain suggests "a likely transition toward endemic circulation," and the agency recommends that people at risk of exposure complete both doses. That recommendation now explicitly includes travelers heading to countries with ongoing clade I or clade II transmission. Gaps in the Data That Deserve Attention Both reports carry limitations that the agency states directly, and readers should weigh them. The air travel analysis was small. Sixty contacts across five flights is a small base, and health departments managed to interview only 29 of them. The absence of detected transmission in a small sample is weaker evidence than its absence in a large one, though it points in the same direction as the much larger clade II investigation. The hospitalization finding is also less precise than the headline number suggests. The 9.73 figure has a 95 percent confidence interval ranging from 2.93 to 60.65, which is wide enough that the true effect could be much smaller or much larger. The direction is clear; the magnitude is not. The surveillance report relies on passive reporting, so mild infections that do not prompt a medical visit are not captured, and total infections are likely undercounted. Missing data were substantial, with vaccination status absent for 62 percent of cases and HIV status for 68 percent. Analyzing only complete records can introduce selection bias. For households, the reasonable steps are unchanged and modest. Anyone at elevated risk who has not completed the two-dose series can ask a primary care provider, sexual health clinic, or local health department about JYNNEOS, and travelers to affected regions should raise it before departure. People with mpox are advised to delay travel until their illness has resolved. Anyone who develops an unexplained rash after travel or close contact should contact a clinician promptly, mention the exposure, and avoid close physical contact until evaluated. Rapidly worsening symptoms, difficulty breathing, or severe pain warrant urgent care. The agency's recommendations on treatment and vaccination remain the same regardless of clade. The agency updates its monthly U.S. case data in the first week of every month. Read more NIH Plans to Bar Scientists on Visas from the Award That Launches Independent Labs A Smuggling Prosecution Over Inactivated Mpox Samples Has Scientists Warning About Outbreak Preparedness Africa CDC Says Contact Tracing Is Not Working in Congo Ebola Outbreak as Deaths Pass 1,700 Key Questions Answered Can someone catch mpox from a passenger on their flight? Investigations to date have not identified any such case. Among 60 contacts of three infected clade I travelers on five flights, no secondary cases were found, and a larger clade II investigation of 1,538 contacts also found none. Why did the CDC stop tracing airline contacts? Because repeated investigations found no evidence of onboard transmission. The agency discontinued aircraft contact investigations for all mpox clades and subclades in 2025. Does that mean mpox is not a travel concern? No. Travel-associated introductions are rising, and the agency documented 21 importations across 2024 and 2025. The risk is tied to close contact at the destination rather than to the flight itself. Who faces the greatest risk of severe illness? People who are unvaccinated and people living with HIV. Unvaccinated patients had 9.73 times the odds of hospitalization compared with fully vaccinated patients, though the confidence interval around that estimate is wide. Should travelers get vaccinated before an international trip? The CDC recommends the two-dose JYNNEOS series for people at risk of exposure, including travelers to countries with ongoing clade I or clade II transmission. A clinician or local health department can advise on individual eligibility. What symptoms should prompt a call to a clinician? An unexplained rash or lesions, particularly following travel or close physical contact, along with fever, swollen lymph nodes, body aches, or exhaustion. Mention any recent travel when seeking care. How current are these numbers? The national surveillance figures cover cases through December 31, 2025, and are provisional. The count of more than 40 clade I cases reflects the agency's situation summary page as currently posted. analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: 5,322 confirmed and probable cases were reported across 2024 and 2025, with 21 separate importations of the virus into the country. The risk of transmission during air travel is considered low for clade I, consistent with earlier findings for clade II.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: The CDC discontinued aircraft contact tracing for all mpox clades and subclades in 2025. analysis.brief_en: The CDC has concluded that the risk of mpox transmission during air travel is low, based on genomic and epidemiologic data. This decision followed the discontinuation of aircraft contact tracing for all mpox clades and subclades in 2025. The agency's latest analysis, published on August 24, 2026, reported 5,322 confirmed and probable cases across 2024 and 2025, with 21 separate importations of the virus into the country. The findings align with earlier conclusions that clade I transmission during air travel is unlikely, as most mpox cases spread through close, sustained physical contact with lesions, scabs, or contaminated items, and not through brief interactions on planes. The CDC emphasized that factors such as vaccination status, destination, and the nature of contact at the destination are more critical in assessing travel risk than the act of flying itself.

news.content: Skip to main content BREAKING Rare August rainfall makes way for plummeting temps in Bay Area forecast News|Bay Area & State SF: Health Officials Renew Mpox Vaccine Push By Bay City News ServiceAug 26, 2026 A colorized transmission electron micrograph shows two mature mpox (monkeypox) virus particles (pink) attached to the surface of an infected VERO E6 cell (blue/teal). The image was captured at the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) Integrated Research Facility (IRF) in Fort Detrick, Maryland. (National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases/National Institutes of Health via Bay City News) National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases/National Institutes of Health/National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases/National Institutes of Health via Bay City News With the Folsom Street Fair about a month away and more than 70 mpox cases reported in San Francisco this year, city health officials this week urged people to get vaccinated and watch for symptoms. The Folsom Street Fair is scheduled for Sept. 27 from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. in San Francisco's South of Market neighborhood, according to organizers. The San Francisco Department of Public Health issued the advisory ahead of the fair, saying there is still time for people who haven't been vaccinated to begin the two-dose series. Advertisement Article continues below this ad As of Monday, more than 70 cases of mpox had been reported in San Francisco in 2026, including eight cases of clade I mpox, according to the Department of Public Health. The department confirmed the city's first clade I case, one of the two types of mpox, on April 14. The case involved an unvaccinated adult who was hospitalized and improving when health officials announced it two days later. The person reported close contact with someone who had traveled internationally. The department says all confirmed clade I cases in San Francisco so far have been associated with international travel. Clade I may cause more severe illness than clade II, which caused a large U.S. outbreak in 2022. Both spread primarily through close skin-to-skin contact, including during sexual activity, and can cause similar symptoms. Both clade strands can cause similar symptoms such as fever, swollen lymph nodes or fatigue, followed by a rash that can resemble pimples or blisters and may be painful. The department recommends that people who develop a rash that looks like mpox contact a health care provider for testing and notify partners who may have been exposed. Advertisement Article continues below this ad Anyone can contract mpox, but the department said most reported U.S. cases have been among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men, as well as transgender people who have sex with men. "While we are in a much better place than we were during the 2022 outbreak, mpox infections can and still do occur," San Francisco Health Officer Dr. Susan Philip said in the department's advisory. Photograph: Vincent Tremeau/Unicef Children make up half of suspected mpox cases in Guinea-Bissau as epidemic spreads West African country reports 46 suspected cases in outbreak declared in July, amid fears virus may be spreading undetected More than half of the mpox cases reported in Guinea-Bissau have been among children, local authorities have said, almost two months since the country announced an epidemic. A national outbreak was declared on 4 July, just over a week after a 27-year-old woman became the first confirmed case of mpox in the west African country. Since then, there have been seven confirmed cases and 46 suspected cases. Half of those patients have been children, with 16 under the age of four. In a statement on Thursday, Unicef warned that because the country’s health surveillance systems were fragile, the virus is probably spreading undetected, leaving even more children at risk. Sandra Martins, the country’s deputy representative for Unicef, said: “This is the first time mpox cases have been reported in Guinea-Bissau, making even a small outbreak a major public health event.” Mpox is an infectious viral disease that can be transmitted through close contact. There have been more than 2,000 mpox-related deaths among tens of thousands of cases recorded across east, central and west Africa since January 2024. Health workers say the Clade variants are consistent with viruses circulating in neighbouring countries, meaning that a risk of cross‐border transmission in the region remains strong. The vast majority of confirmed cases are in the Bissau autonomous sector, where the capital is, while one case is in the nearby Biombo area. No deaths have been reported to date. Dr Magda Robalo, a former health minister who led the country’s Covid-19 response, said that to eliminate the “biggest gaps in the health system right now”, increased surveillance would have to be prioritised and frontline capacity reinforced. “Even though the numbers are small, new cases have appeared intermittently over several weeks, which means transmission is ongoing,” said Robalo, who is also co-founder of the Institute for Global Health and Development and former director of communicable diseases for the World Health Organization. The outbreak comes as the country grapples with infrastructure challenges and the aftermath of the suspension of last November’s presidential election by the military, which remains in power. There was no electricity throughout Thursday in Bissau for instance because of petrol scarcity since the weekend. First malaria drug for babies is approved in ‘major public health milestone’ Read more Many public health laboratories in the region lack equipment to deal with epidemics but have institutional knowledge from handling other crises. In Guinea-Bissau, that is no different but there is also a sense of urgency, with primary schools scheduled to reopen across the country in September. After the outbreak was declared, community health workers immediately began a door-to-door public awareness campaign with megaphones and translated leaflets, supported by the health ministry and international agencies. These grassroots initiatives are seen as vital for building public trust in the public health sector. Earlier this year, the country suspended a controversial US-funded trial on hepatitis B vaccinations for newborns, citing ethical concerns and procedural flaws. The decision was lauded by many across the continent and has highlighted sensitivities around emergency health interventions. analysis.brief_en: In Guinea-Bissau, children account for half of the suspected mpox cases as an epidemic spreads. The national outbreak was declared on 4 July 2026, following the first confirmed case in the country. As of August 2026, there have been 46 suspected cases and 7 confirmed cases, with no deaths reported. Local authorities and health workers are concerned that the virus may be spreading undetected due to the country’s fragile health surveillance systems. The outbreak has prompted urgent public health measures, including a door-to-door awareness campaign supported by the health ministry and international agencies. The risk of cross-border transmission remains high, as the clade variants align with those in neighboring countries. Efforts are underway to strengthen surveillance and frontline capacity to address the ongoing transmission and mitigate the impact on children, who are disproportionately affected.

news.content_title: Mpox spreads to further groups of people in Berlin
news.content: The mpox virus is increasingly being transmitted in Berlin through sex between men and women. According to the State Office for Health and Social Affairs (Lageso), several cases have recently been reported in connection with sex-positive events for heterosexual and queer people, as stated in Lageso's latest weekly report. So far in August, two women with mpox have been reported to Lageso. According to the authority, a man also became infected during the same period, stating that he may have contracted the virus during sex with a woman. All three are thought to have become infected through anonymous sexual encounters in clubs or at home. A total of four cases of mpox in women have been reported to Lageso so far this year. In fact, it is primarily men who have sex with men and frequently change sexual partners who become infected. The total number of mpox cases reported in Berlin so far this year stands at 156. This is more than in the same period last year (144) and significantly more than in the whole of 2024 (38) or 2023 (13). According to the Robert Koch Institute (RKI), the German public health agency, 375 cases of mpox have been reported across Germany so far this year (as of August 27). A total of 98% of these were men, epidemiologist Klaus Jansen from the RKI told the dpa. The men for whom the route of infection is known contracted the virus almost exclusively through sex with men. "Across Germany, we are not currently seeing a trend similar to the situation described by Lageso for Berlin." Infectious diseases epidemiologist Claudia Ruscher from Lageso said: "It is a cause of great concern to us that mpox is spreading to another group of people who previously appeared unaffected and who are therefore largely unvaccinated and poorly informed." Four women might initially seem like a small number, but there is a new dynamic at play here. The infections occurred within a short space of time. In recent years, either no women at all or just one woman per year had been infected. Only during the major outbreak in 2022 were there a total of four cases among women. However, the total number of cases in that outbreak was around ten times higher than it is at present. People who are unvaccinated and contracting mpox for the first time are more likely to experience a more severe course of the disease. "They are more likely to have a feverish illness and often develop skin lesions all over their body," said Ruscher. "These are not just blisters, but itchy pustules, some of which are also pus-filled. They are really very painful." Mpox is a viral disease and is transmitted through close physical contact, particularly during sex. news.content: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages August 1, 2026 - August 30, 2026 GO Home Taiwan News Wed, Aug 26, 2026 page2 CDC reports first two local cases of new mpox strain By Hou Chia-yu and Sam Garcia / Staff reporter, with staff writer Add TT as Preferred Source Taiwan had two local cases of mpox clade Ib this month, marking the first locally acquired infections of this strain of the virus, the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) said today. The patients, both men in their 30s, are in stable condition and had not received an mpox vaccine before developing symptoms, the CDC said. The first patient developed a fever late last month, followed by a rash and pustules, and was diagnosed with mpox after seeking medical care and undergoing testing, CDC Deputy Director-General Lin Ming-cheng (林明誠) said. A sign displayed at a Centers for Disease Control news conference in Taipei shows information about mpox in an undated photograph. Photo: CNA The second patient developed a rash early this month, followed by fever and muscle aches, with genetic sequencing confirming that both were infected with mpox clade Ib, Lin said. Mpox is a viral infectious disease primarily spread through sexual contact, hugging, kissing or direct skin-to-skin contact, the CDC said. The clade Ib strain has similar symptoms to the more common clade II, including fever, swollen lymph nodes, rashes and blisters, but its rash may be more widespread and it may spread more easily within households, Lin said. Young children, pregnant women and people with chronic illnesses who have weakened immune systems face a higher risk of severe disease, he said. Mpox vaccines remain effective against clade Ib, while the antiviral drug tecovirimat can also be used to treat severe cases, he added. As of Sunday, Taiwan had recorded 28 new mpox cases this year, including 19 locally acquired and nine imported cases, all involving men aged 20 to 50, the CDC said. Since the first imported mpox clade Ib case was reported in May, Taiwan has recorded nine clade Ib infections, including seven imported and now two locally acquired cases, it said. Since Taiwan classified mpox as a Category 2 communicable disease in 2022, the nation has recorded 544 cases, including 500 locally acquired and 44 imported cases, CDC data showed. Most local cases had a history of unprotected sexual activity, with nearly 90 percent unvaccinated against mpox, the CDC said. People engaging in unprotected or risky sexual activity with multiple partners face a higher risk of infection, while the risk to the general population remains low, it said. The mpox vaccine remains the most effective way to prevent infection, Lin said, adding that as of last month, 79,216 people had completed the recommended two doses, while 31,755 people had received only one dose. Two doses provide about 90 percent protection against mpox, compared with 40 to 80 percent after one dose, so those considered at-risk should complete the two-dose series as soon as possible, he said. There are currently 318 medical institutions nationwide offering government-funded mpox vaccines. People who have engaged in high-risk sexual activity within the past year, have had a sexually transmitted infection or have a sexual partner with related risk factors are eligible for the government-funded vaccine. Mpox has an incubation period of up to 21 days, and some people may be infectious one to four days before symptoms appear, the CDC said. People who develop rashes, blisters or pustules along with fever, headaches, muscle aches or swollen lymph nodes should wear a mask and seek medical attention, and inform their doctor of any travel, exposure and contact history, it said. news.content: Crime & Safety SF Health Officials Renew Mpox Vaccine Push The San Francisco Department of Public Health issued the advisory ahead of the Folsom Street Fair. Bay City News , News Partner Posted Wed, Aug 26, 2026 at 2:21 pm PT Read More SAN FRANCISCO, CA With the Folsom Street Fair about a month away and more than 70 mpox cases reported in San Francisco this year, city health officials this week urged people to get vaccinated and watch for symptoms. The Folsom Street Fair is scheduled for Sept. 27 from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m. in San Francisco's South of Market neighborhood, according to organizers. The San Francisco Department of Public Health issued the advisory ahead of the fair, saying there is still time for people who haven't been vaccinated to begin the two-dose series. As of Monday, more than 70 cases of mpox had been reported in San Francisco in 2026, including eight cases of clade I mpox, according to the Department of Public Health. Find out what's happening in San Francisco for free with the latest updates from Patch. The department confirmed the city's first clade I case, one of the two types of mpox, on April 14. The case involved an unvaccinated adult who was hospitalized and improving when health officials announced it two days later. The person reported close contact with someone who had traveled internationally. The department says all confirmed clade I cases in San Francisco so far have been associated with international travel. Clade I may cause more severe illness than clade II, which caused a large U.S. outbreak in 2022. Find out what's happening in San Francisco for free with the latest updates from Patch. Both spread primarily through close skin-to-skin contact, including during sexual activity, and can cause similar symptoms. Both clade strands can cause similar symptoms such as fever, swollen lymph nodes or fatigue, followed by a rash that can resemble pimples or blisters and may be painful. The department recommends that people who develop a rash that looks like mpox contact a health care provider for testing and notify partners who may have been exposed. Anyone can contract mpox, but the department said most reported U.S. cases have been among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men, as well as transgender people who have sex with men. "While we are in a much better place than we were during the 2022 outbreak, mpox infections can and still do occur," San Francisco Health Officer Dr. Susan Philip said in the department's advisory. Health officials are encouraging people at risk for mpox, including those planning to travel to parts of Africa and Europe where clade I has been reported, to receive both doses of the vaccine. The second dose can be given at least 28 days after the first, and the department says people who wait longer than 28 days don't need to restart the series. Booster doses aren't currently recommended for people who have completed both doses, and vaccination is not recommended at this time for people who previously had mpox. Dr. Julia Janssen, deputy director of the department's sexually transmitted infection and HIV branch, said vaccination reduces the chance of infection and helps protect against severe illness, hospitalization and death. The department also says the vaccine can be given to people who are immunocompromised, including people living with HIV or taking medications that suppress the immune system. Health officials cautioned that vaccination does not eliminate the possibility of infection. Fully vaccinated people should still watch for symptoms and seek testing if they develop them. The vaccine is available through health care providers and local pharmacies. The Department of Public Health directs people without insurance or those having difficulty finding a vaccine to its mpox information and vaccination resources at sf.gov/mpox. Mpox Surge in Guinea-Bissau: Why Children Are Being Hit? Written by Dr. R.S Janani Reviewed by The Medindia News Review Team on Aug 25 2026 12:48 PM Busy? Tap to listen instead of reading 0:00/0:00 A new mpox outbreak is putting children in focus as health authorities investigate suspected infections and work to contain the virus in Guinea-Bissau. Guinea-Bissau is confronting its first-ever mpox outbreak, with 46 suspected cases reported and 23 involving children under 15. UNICEF says 16 of the suspected pediatric cases are children aged 0-4, raising concern over the risk of severe complications. The outbreak was declared on July 4, 2026, and seven cases had been confirmed among adults by August 17. UNICEF has warned that fragile disease surveillance could mean additional infections are going undetected. (1✔ ✔Trusted Source Children account for half of suspected mpox cases in Guinea-Bissau Go to source) WHO Detects Hybrid Mpox Virus After Two Monkeypox Strains Combine WHO detects hybrid mpox strain combining clades Ib and IIb and calls for strengthened surveillance amid ongoing global outbreak activity. Guinea-Bissau Reports Its First Mpox Outbreak Guinea-Bissau declared its first-ever mpox outbreak on July 4, 2026. By August 17, the country had reported seven confirmed cases, all among adults. Six cases were in Bissau, and one was in the Biombo Region. No deaths had been reported. The outbreak is attracting particular attention because of the number of suspected cases among children. Mpox Cases Expanding Beyond At-Risk Groups The 2024 Mpox outbreak is spreading beyond traditional at-risk groups, affecting a broader demographic globally compared to the 2022 outbreak. Half of Suspected Mpox Cases Are Children Of the 46 suspected mpox cases, 23 were children under 15, meaning children account for half of all suspected cases. Sixteen of these children were between 0 and 4 years old. Young children are a major concern because they can be more vulnerable to complications from mpox. The reopening of schools in September could also increase close contact among children and create more opportunities for mpox transmission. When children make up half of suspected cases, every missed infection matters. Which Crucial Protein Elicited Mpox Vaccine Through AI? A novel AI model helped find a key protein, named OPG153, in monkeypox virus, which could lead to cheaper and simple vaccine or a new antibody drug design. Why Health Officials Are Worried About Hidden Transmission? Another concern is that the confirmed mpox (monkeypox) cases do not appear to be linked to one another. This raises the possibility that there are undetected chains of transmission in the community. Guinea-Bissau also has gaps in community surveillance, testing, contact tracing, and identifying how the virus is spreading. These challenges can make it harder to find infections before they spread further. UNICEF is supporting the Ministry of Public Health, WHO, and other partners with surveillance, contact tracing, infection prevention, and community awareness. The sooner an infection is found, the easier it is to stop the chain. Is Monkeypox the Next Pandemic? Mpox (Monkeypox) is spreading worldwide, but is it as dangerous as COVID-19? Explore the facts and WHO's stance on this growing health concern. Mpox Explained: What Causes It, and How Does the Virus Spread? Mpox is an infectious disease caused by the mpox virus, which belongs to the Orthopoxvirus family. It can cause A rash or skin lesions Fever Swollen lymph nodes Headache Muscle aches Tiredness Most people recover, but some can develop serious illness. The virus mainly spreads through close physical contact with an infected person, particularly contact with skin lesions, body fluids, or respiratory secretions. It can also spread through contaminated clothing, bedding, and other materials. Mpox can also spread from infected animals to humans through direct contact. During pregnancy, the virus can pass from an infected pregnant person to the fetus or newborn. What Happens Next? Health authorities are focusing on early detection, testing, contact tracing, and infection prevention to slow the spread of mpox in Guinea-Bissau. Families are being encouraged to seek medical care quickly if a child or other family member develops a rash, fever, swollen lymph nodes, or other possible mpox symptoms. UNICEF says it needs more than US$150,000 in emergency funding to support key parts of the mpox response, including disease surveillance, prevention, and care. Strengthening these efforts will be important as health teams continue to look for new infections. (2✔ ✔Trusted Source Mpox Go to source) Every confirmed case gives health workers another chance to break the chain of infection. Guinea-Bissau's mpox outbreak remains limited in confirmed cases, but the high number of suspected infections among children has raised concern. Continued testing, surveillance, and public awareness can help prevent further spread. When it comes to mpox, catching the virus early is better than chasing it later. news.title_zh: 猴痘 几内亚比绍激增:为何儿童遭到袭击?
news.source_body_en: Guinea-Bissau is experiencing its first-ever mpox outbreak, with 46 suspected cases reported as of August 17, 2026. Among these, 23 cases involved children under 15, with 16 specifically aged 0-4, raising concerns about the risk of severe complications in young children. The outbreak was declared on July 4, 2026, and seven confirmed cases were reported, all among adults. Health authorities are emphasizing early detection, testing, and contact tracing to contain the virus, as the lack of clear transmission links suggests possible undetected chains of spread. UNICEF is supporting the Ministry of Public Health and WHO with surveillance, prevention, and community awareness efforts. The reopening of schools in September could increase close contact among children, potentially facilitating further transmission. No deaths have been reported, but the high proportion of pediatric cases has prompted urgent action to prevent the spread of mpox in the country.

Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% Angolan public health authorities have officially confirmed the first positive case of Mpox in the northwestern province of Bengo, escalating concerns over the steady proliferation of the viral disease across the southern African nation. The formal confirmation marks a critical turning point in regional epidemiological containment strategies, as provincial borders become increasingly porous to viral transmission. Josefa Gomes, the head of the Public Health Department at the Provincial Health Office in Bengo, announced the positive diagnosis to the press on Thursday. The confirmation shatters a period of cautious optimism in the province, which had previously recorded negative laboratory results for three suspected pediatric cases in the adjacent Icolo e Bengo municipality in June 2026. The shift from suspected to confirmed status underscores the rapid evolution of the continental health emergency, prompting immediate reviews of national resource allocation and disease surveillance protocols. National Epidemiological Landscape The confirmed case in Bengo is not an isolated incident but rather the latest data point in a growing national health crisis. Angolan authorities have been battling a persistent Mpox outbreak that has stubbornly expanded despite targeted interventions. Epidemiological data paints a concerning picture of the viral spread across multiple administrative zones. Since November 2024, the Angolan Ministry of Health has officially recorded 14 confirmed cases of Mpox nationwide. Within the past week, the oil-rich enclave of Cabinda reported seven new confirmed infections within a 24-hour window. Simultaneously, the northern province of Zaire documented six new cases, predominantly affecting adolescents and young adults aged 15 to 19 from the Tando Zinze, Liambo, and Ngoio municipalities. To date, suspected cases have triggered epidemiological investigations in at least five distinct provinces, draining laboratory resources at the National Institute of Health Research in Luanda. The concentration of recent cases in border provinces like Zaire and Cabinda highlights the vulnerability of cross-border transit routes. Prior to the confirmed infection in Bengo, local health administrators had proactively initiated preemptive vaccination campaigns. These drives targeted high-risk demographics, including frontline healthcare workers, defense and security personnel, and residents in border municipalities such as Ambriz, Nambuangongo, Muxaluando, and Quicunzo. Overlapping Public Health Crises The Mpox escalation arrives at a highly precarious moment for the Angolan healthcare system, which is simultaneously grappling with a severe cholera epidemic. According to recent situational reports from the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), cholera infections have penetrated 17 of Angola's 21 provinces. The epicenters of the cholera outbreak, including Luanda, Cuanza Norte, and crucially, Bengo and Icolo e Bengo, account for approximately 98 percent of all reported cases. The dual burden of Mpox and cholera is stretching provincial medical infrastructure to its absolute limits. The Africa CDC has deployed specialized incidence management teams to Luanda to assist in coordinating the multidisciplinary response. However, the convergence of a waterborne bacterial outbreak with a contact-transmitted viral epidemic necessitates fundamentally different logistical supply chains, complicating the distribution of vaccines, therapeutics, and personal protective equipment. The financial toll on the state budget is mounting, with contingency funds being rapidly depleted to sustain dual-track epidemiological surveillance. Global and East African Implications The steady march of the Mpox virus through Angola carries significant implications for the broader African continent and global health security networks. For East African nations, particularly Kenya and Uganda, the Angolan outbreak serves as a stark warning regarding the speed of regional transmission. The Central Bank of Kenya estimates that cross-border trade disruptions caused by health emergencies can severely impact regional gross domestic product. If the outbreak necessitates border closures or strict quarantine measures within the Southern African Development Community (SADC), supply chain bottlenecks could artificially inflate commodity prices across the continent. From an economic perspective, the mobilization of domestic health resources diverts critical funding away from infrastructure and development projects. The cost of deploying comprehensive vaccination rings and maintaining strict isolation wards runs into millions of dollars. For instance, equivalent public health mobilizations in Kenya routinely cost upwards of KES 4.5 billion to sustain over a fiscal quarter. The Angolan government must now balance these immediate health expenditures against long-term economic stability. As the Ministry of Health works to trace the contacts of the Bengo patient, the international community watches closely. The efficacy of Angola's localized containment strategy will likely inform global best practices for managing concurrent infectious disease outbreaks in resource-constrained environments. Without rapid intervention and sustained international support, the localized clusters in Bengo, Zaire, and Cabinda risk coalescing into a nationwide epidemic. How did this story land? For instance, equivalent public health mobilizations in Kenya routinely cost upwards of KES 4.5 billion to sustain over a fiscal quarter. The Angolan government must now balance these immediate health expenditures against long-term economic stability. As the Ministry of Health works to trace the contacts of the Bengo patient, the international community watches closely. The efficacy of Angola's localized containment strategy will likely inform global best practices for managing concurrent infectious disease outbreaks in resource-constrained environments. Without rapid intervention and sustained international support, the localized clusters in Bengo, Zaire, and Cabinda risk coalescing into a nationwide epidemic. How did this story land? Ahead of San Francisco's slate of gatherings and shows, city health officials are reminding at-risk residents to get fully vaccinated against mpox. Here’s how to find an mpox vaccine. Aug 27, 2026 Updated 12:16 pm PT Carlos Cabrera-LomelíCarly Severn Ria Garcia, licensed vocational nurse with the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, draws up mpox vaccines at the Balboa Sports Complex vaccine site in Encino on Sept. 8, 2022. (Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images) Ahead of San Francisco’s jam-packed fall slate of gatherings and concerts — including Folsom Street and Portola Music Festival — city health officials are reminding at-risk residents to get fully vaccinated against mpox. The San Francisco Department of Public Health confirmed on Tuesday that over 70 cases of mpox — formerly known as monkeypox — have been reported in San Francisco this year. Eight of these infections involve clade I mpox: a strain that in other parts of the world has caused more severe symptoms than the clade II strain associated with the 2022 outbreak in the Bay Area. According to SFDPH, mpox cases usually increase in summer and fall — especially when the city is hosting events that draw people from all over the world. “People come together, they’re meeting,” said Dr. Julia Janssen, deputy director of the STI and HIV branch at SFDPH. “That’s why we emphasize and recommend the Jynneos vaccine during this time.” Thousands of people dance as Disclosure performs at Portola Music Festival in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2024. (Estefany Gonzalez for KQED) Ahead of San Francisco Pride celebrations back in June, health officials recommended the mpox vaccine — which has the brand name Jynneos — to the same at-risk populations that have been most affected by previous mpox outbreaks. These included gay and bisexual men, along with transgender people who have sex with men. But the fact that the clade I strain is also starting to spread among local populations in popular tourist destinations — including Italy, Spain and Portugal — has prompted San Francisco health officials to now recommend that more people beyond those primary at-risk groups get vaccinated if they’re planning to travel to these areas. “We have started to see local transmission in Western Europe,” Janssen said. “We recommend that anyone traveling outside of the United States — particularly to a country where clade I mpox is spreading between people — and [who] anticipates having sex during travel: Get the Jynneos vaccine.” The recommendation is also extended to Bay Area folks who have sex here with anyone who has just traveled to those areas. “There’s currently no evidence of local clade I transmission within San Francisco,” Janssen said. All confirmed clade I mpox cases in the city have been associated with international travel. ‘The absolute best protection’ The symptoms of clade I and clade II mpox are similar and can initially resemble the flu. The virus also appears as a rash or sores or spots that resemble pimples or blisters on the skin anywhere on the body, including the face, inside the mouth, hands, feet, chest, genitals and anus. Related Article Clade I mpox, however, has historically caused more severe disease and more deaths in other countries, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. During the 2022 outbreak, more than 15,000 San Francisco residents received both doses of the mpox vaccine. “That led to a dramatic decrease in cases,” Janssen said. “We’re in a much better place now because of the uptake of the Jynneos vaccine in San Francisco.” She called the vaccine “really the absolute best protection” and “the main tool in our toolbox.” Both clade I and clade II usually spread through close skin-to-skin contact, including sex. Anyone can get mpox, but most cases in the United States are among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men, as well as transgender people who have sex with men. On the heels of SDFPH’s advisory, here’s what to know about mpox and the Jynneos vaccine in the Bay Area this fall. Who’s eligible for an mpox vaccine in the Bay Area? The vaccine currently available in the U.S. (brand name: Jynneos) is a two-dose series, with roughly a month between doses. Maximal immunity will build two weeks after your second dose. The vaccine “protects against both clade 1 and clade 2 mpox,” Janssen said, and added that if someone just got one dose in the past, they may just need the second dose now. “Anyone who has received one dose can go ahead and receive their second dose if it has been 28 days or more since their first dose,” she said. “There’s no need to restart.” The Leather Pride flag flies at the Folsom Street Fair in San Francisco on Sept. 30, 2018. (Michelle Wiley/KQED) The CDC recommends the two-dose mpox vaccine to gay and bisexual men and other men who have sex with men, as well as transgender, nonbinary or gender-diverse people who in the past 6 months have had: More than one sexual partner and/or A new diagnosis of one or more sexually transmitted infections. The CDC’s vaccine recommendations also include anyone who has had sex at a commercial sex venue like a sex club or bathhouse. See the CDC’s full mpox vaccine eligibility recommendations. San Francisco additionally recommends vaccination for anyone living with HIV, anyone taking PrEP or who’s eligible to take it and sex workers. What about travel and mpox? In 2025, SFDPH expanded their mpox vaccine recommendations to include anyone traveling outside the U.S. — particularly to a country where clade I mpox is spreading between people — who anticipates having sex while they travel. The CDC recommends getting both doses of the Jynneos vaccine “if you anticipate experiencing any of the following” while traveling to these countries: Warren Manio, 36, sits on top of his friend’s shoulders as Natasha Bedingfield performs at Portola Music Festival in San Francisco on Sept. 28, 2024. (Estefany Gonzalez for KQED) Sex with a new partner Sex at a commercial sex venue, such as a sex club or bathhouse Sex in exchange for money, goods, drugs or other trade Sex in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party or festival. As of August this year, SFDPH also recommends that if you’re a Bay Area resident who is having sex with a person who’s traveled to these countries, you should also seek out the vaccine. The mpox vaccine was also originally only available for people aged 18 and older, but in 2022, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued an emergency-use authorization that allows providers to also give the vaccine to young people aged under 18 who are “determined to be at high risk” of infection. Where can I find an mpox vaccine? If you have a regular health care provider, SFDPH recommends you ask them first about getting the mpox vaccine. Your vaccine will be free, but you may be charged a regular copay for seeing your provider. If you’re eligible for the vaccine, your health insurance should cover the costs thanks to the CDC’s recommendations. If you don’t have a regular health care provider or insurance, SFDPH said you can visit one of these four pharmacies in the city (two Walgreens and two CVS locations). A vial of the mpox vaccine is displayed by a medical professional at a vaccination site in July, 2022. (James Carbone/Newsday RM via Getty Images) (As with the COVID-19 vaccine, receiving an mpox vaccine won’t make you a public charge or affect any future immigration processes you may enter into, and you won’t be asked about your immigration status to receive the mpox vaccine.) If you get your health care through a health system like Kaiser Permanente, it’s unlikely you’ll be able to get your mpox vaccine covered by insurance at a pharmacy like CVS or Walgreens — the way you can’t get your COVID-19 or flu shot covered by Kaiser at a pharmacy either — and may have to seek it directly from a Kaiser provider. If you’re able to make an appointment online at a pharmacy for your mpox vaccine, you should consider calling that location ahead of time to verify that they do indeed have supplies in stock. Ahead of San Francisco's slate of gatherings and shows, city health officials are reminding at-risk residents to get fully vaccinated against mpox. Here’s how to find an mpox vaccine. Aug 27, 2026 Updated 12:16 pm PT Carlos Cabrera-LomelíCarly Severn Ria Garcia, licensed vocational nurse with the Los Angeles County Department of Public Health, draws up mpox vaccines at the Balboa Sports Complex vaccine site in Encino on Sept. 8, 2022. (Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Los Angeles Daily News via Getty Images) Ahead of San Francisco’s jam-packed fall slate of gatherings and concerts — including Folsom Street and Portola Music Festival — city health officials are reminding at-risk residents to get fully vaccinated against mpox. The San Francisco Department of Public Health confirmed on Tuesday that over 70 cases of mpox — formerly known as monkeypox — have been reported in San Francisco this year. Eight of these infections involve clade I mpox: a strain that in other parts of the world has caused more severe symptoms than the clade II strain associated with the 2022 outbreak in the Bay Area. According to SFDPH, mpox cases usually increase in summer and fall — especially when the city is hosting events that draw people from all over the world. “People come together, they’re meeting,” said Dr. Julia Janssen, deputy director of the STI and HIV branch at SFDPH. “That’s why we emphasize and recommend the Jynneos vaccine during this time.” Thousands of people dance as Disclosure performs at Portola Music Festival in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2024. (Estefany Gonzalez for KQED) Ahead of San Francisco Pride celebrations back in June, health officials recommended the mpox vaccine — which has the brand name Jynneos — to the same at-risk populations that have been most affected by previous mpox outbreaks. These included gay and bisexual men, along with transgender people who have sex with men. But the fact that the clade I strain is also starting to spread among local populations in popular tourist destinations — including Italy, Spain and Portugal — has prompted San Francisco health officials to now recommend that more people beyond those primary at-risk groups get vaccinated if they’re planning to travel to these areas. “We have started to see local transmission in Western Europe,” Janssen said. “We recommend that anyone traveling outside of the United States — particularly to a country where clade I mpox is spreading between people — and [who] anticipates having sex during travel: Get the Jynneos vaccine.” The recommendation is also extended to Bay Area folks who have sex here with anyone who has just traveled to those areas. “There’s currently no evidence of local clade I transmission within San Francisco,” Janssen said. All confirmed clade I mpox cases in the city have been associated with international travel. ‘The absolute best protection’ The symptoms of clade I and clade II mpox are similar and can initially resemble the flu. The virus also appears as a rash or sores or spots that resemble pimples or blisters on the skin anywhere on the body, including the face, inside the mouth, hands, feet, chest, genitals and anus. Related Article Clade I mpox, however, has historically caused more severe disease and more deaths in other countries, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. During the 2022 outbreak, more than 15,000 San Francisco residents received both doses of the mpox vaccine. “That led to a dramatic decrease in cases,” Janssen said. “We’re in a much better place now because of the uptake of the Jynneos vaccine in San Francisco.” She called the vaccine “really the absolute best protection” and “the main tool in our toolbox.” Both clade I and clade II usually spread through close skin-to-skin contact, including sex. Anyone can get mpox, but most cases in the United States are among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men, as well as transgender people who have sex with men. On the heels of SDFPH’s advisory, here’s what to know about mpox and the Jynneos vaccine in the Bay Area this fall. Who’s eligible for an mpox vaccine in the Bay Area? The vaccine currently available in the U.S. (brand name: Jynneos) is a two-dose series, with roughly a month between doses. Maximal immunity will build two weeks after your second dose. The vaccine “protects against both clade 1 and clade 2 mpox,” Janssen said, and added that if someone just got one dose in the past, they may just need the second dose now. “Anyone who has received one dose can go ahead and receive their second dose if it has been 28 days or more since their first dose,” she said. “There’s no need to restart.” The Leather Pride flag flies at the Folsom Street Fair in San Francisco on Sept. 30, 2018. (Michelle Wiley/KQED) The CDC recommends the two-dose mpox vaccine to gay and bisexual men and other men who have sex with men, as well as transgender, nonbinary or gender-diverse people who in the past 6 months have had: More than one sexual partner and/or A new diagnosis of one or more sexually transmitted infections. The CDC’s vaccine recommendations also include anyone who has had sex at a commercial sex venue like a sex club or bathhouse. See the CDC’s full mpox vaccine eligibility recommendations. San Francisco additionally recommends vaccination for anyone living with HIV, anyone taking PrEP or who’s eligible to take it and sex workers. What about travel and mpox? In 2025, SFDPH expanded their mpox vaccine recommendations to include anyone traveling outside the U.S. — particularly to a country where clade I mpox is spreading between people — who anticipates having sex while they travel. The CDC recommends getting both doses of the Jynneos vaccine “if you anticipate experiencing any of the following” while traveling to these countries: Warren Manio, 36, sits on top of his friend’s shoulders as Natasha Bedingfield performs at Portola Music Festival in San Francisco on Sept. 28, 2024. (Estefany Gonzalez for KQED) Sex with a new partner Sex at a commercial sex venue, such as a sex club or bathhouse Sex in exchange for money, goods, drugs or other trade Sex in association with a large public event, such as a rave, party or festival. As of August this year, SFDPH also recommends that if you’re a Bay Area resident who is having sex with a person who’s traveled to these countries, you should also seek out the vaccine. The mpox vaccine was also originally only available for people aged 18 and older, but in 2022, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued an emergency-use authorization that allows providers to also give the vaccine to young people aged under 18 who are “determined to be at high risk” of infection. Where can I find an mpox vaccine? If you have a regular health care provider, SFDPH recommends you ask them first about getting the mpox vaccine. Your vaccine will be free, but you may be charged a regular copay for seeing your provider. If you’re eligible for the vaccine, your health insurance should cover the costs thanks to the CDC’s recommendations. If you don’t have a regular health care provider or insurance, SFDPH said you can visit one of these four pharmacies in the city (two Walgreens and two CVS locations). A vial of the mpox vaccine is displayed by a medical professional at a vaccination site in July, 2022. (James Carbone/Newsday RM via Getty Images) (As with the COVID-19 vaccine, receiving an mpox vaccine won’t make you a public charge or affect any future immigration processes you may enter into, and you won’t be asked about your immigration status to receive the mpox vaccine.) If you get your health care through a health system like Kaiser Permanente, it’s unlikely you’ll be able to get your mpox vaccine covered by insurance at a pharmacy like CVS or Walgreens — the way you can’t get your COVID-19 or flu shot covered by Kaiser at a pharmacy either — and may have to seek it directly from a Kaiser provider. If you’re able to make an appointment online at a pharmacy for your mpox vaccine, you should consider calling that location ahead of time to verify that they do indeed have supplies in stock. analysis.brief_en: San Francisco health officials are urging at-risk residents to get vaccinated against mpox ahead of the fall party season, which includes events like the Folsom Street and Portola Music Festival. The San Francisco Department of Public Health confirmed over 70 cases of mpox this year, with eight involving clade I, a strain linked to more severe symptoms in other regions. Officials note that mpox cases typically rise during summer and fall due to increased social gatherings. They recommend the Jynneos vaccine, which protects against both clade I and clade II mpox, especially for those planning to travel to areas where clade I is spreading. While there is no evidence of local clade I transmission in San Francisco, all confirmed cases are associated with international travel. The vaccine is a two-dose series, with maximal immunity building two weeks after the second dose. Health officials emphasize that the vaccine is the best protection available and that individuals who have already received one dose should get the second dose if it has been 28 days or more since the first.

An image created during an investigation into an outbreak of monkeypox, which took place in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 1996 to 1997, shows the arms and torso of a patient with skin lesions due to monkeypox, in this undated image obtained by Reuters on May 18, 2022. CDC/Brian W.J. Mahy/Handout via Reuters INFO The Department of Health says that monkeypox has not been detected in the Philippines or at its borders Play Video MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Health (DOH) on Friday, May 20, said it was “intensifying” border screening and “ensuring that surveillance systems are actively monitoring the situation” following the detection of monkeypox cases in European countries, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada. The DOH said that monkeypox has not been detected in the Philippines or at its borders. Monkeypox is a viral disease coming from animals “that occurs primarily in tropical rainforest areas of Central and West Africa and is occasionally exported to other regions.” Monkeypox is a virus that causes fever symptoms as well as a distinctive bumpy rash. It is usually mild, although there are two main strains: the Congo strain, which is more severe – with up to 10% mortality – and the West African strain, which has a fatality rate in about 1% of cases. The UK cases have been reported as the West African strain. Symptoms of monkeypox include fever, rash, and swollen lymp nodes, which may lead to a range of medical implications. The DOH urged the public to continue observing minimum health standards to prevent monkeypox transmission. The viral disease is being transmitted to humans through close contact with an infected person, animal, or contaminated materials. “While monkeypox look like smallpox, it is less contagious and causes less severe illness,” the DOH said. Must Read EXPLAINER: Why monkeypox cases are spreading in Europe, US The recent news about monkeypox comes as the Philippines and the rest of the world is still dealing with the COVID-19 pandemic. An image created during an investigation into an outbreak of monkeypox, which took place in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, 1996 to 1997, shows the arms and torso of a patient with skin lesions due to monkeypox, in this undated image obtained by Reuters on May 18, 2022. CDC/Brian W.J. Mahy/Handout via Reuters INFO The Department of Health says that monkeypox has not been detected in the Philippines or at its borders Play Video MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Health (DOH) on Friday, May 20, said it was “intensifying” border screening and “ensuring that surveillance systems are actively monitoring the situation” following the detection of monkeypox cases in European countries, the United States, the United Kingdom, and Canada. The DOH said that monkeypox has not been detected in the Philippines or at its borders. Monkeypox is a viral disease coming from animals “that occurs primarily in tropical rainforest areas of Central and West Africa and is occasionally exported to other regions.” Monkeypox is a virus that causes fever symptoms as well as a distinctive bumpy rash. It is usually mild, although there are two main strains: the Congo strain, which is more severe – with up to 10% mortality – and the West African strain, which has a fatality rate in about 1% of cases. The UK cases have been reported as the West African strain. Symptoms of monkeypox include fever, rash, and swollen lymp nodes, which may lead to a range of medical implications. The DOH urged the public to continue observing minimum health standards to prevent monkeypox transmission. The viral disease is being transmitted to humans through close contact with an infected person, animal, or contaminated materials. “While monkeypox look like smallpox, it is less contagious and causes less severe illness,” the DOH said. Must Read EXPLAINER: Why monkeypox cases are spreading in Europe, US The recent news about monkeypox comes as the Philippines and the rest of the world is still dealing with the COVID-19 pandemic. news.content_title: Health Bureau confirms Macau imported mpox case
news.content: The Health Bureau (SSM) announced in a statement yesterday that it had received a report of one imported mpox* case involving a young male local resident. According to the statement, the patient had developed symptoms including fever, headache, and muscle pain on August 18 while travelling abroad, developing a skin rash the following day and self-medicating without seeking medical attention. When he returned to Macau, the statement said he visited the private Kiang Wu Hospital for consultation and sample collection on Monday, testing positive for mpox. As his symptoms persisted, he subsequently sought care at the public Conde S. Januário Hospital Centre and is currently receiving inpatient treatment. The statement noted that he was in stable condition. The statement added that the patient’s cohabitants have not shown symptoms, though the bureau will still arrange for them to receive the mpox vaccine. The statement pointed out that the patient had, according to epidemiological investigations, engaged in “high-risk sexual behaviour in the Chinese mainland during the incubation period”. He had no high-risk sexual behaviour in Macau or after symptom onset, and denied contact with rodents or primates. He had not been vaccinated for the disease. Mpox, according to the statement, spreads primarily through high-risk sexual behavior – especially among individuals with multiple partners or men who have sex with men—as well as through direct contact with infected skin lesions, contaminated objects, prolonged face-to-face respiratory droplets, or infected animals like rodents and primates. The Health Bureau urged the public to practise safe sex and avoid casual or multiple partners, as well as avoid contact with people, animals, or contaminated items suspected to be infected. Moreover, the bureau said that if symptoms appear, one should immediately seek medical attention, disclose relevant exposure history, and avoid sexual activity or close contact with others, the statement said. The statement added that “high-risk individuals aged 18 or above (including men who have sex with men) may consider getting vaccinated against mpox”. The bureau emphasised that, according to information from the WHO and other regions, general public risk remains low and mass vaccination is unnecessary. The statement said it carries a low global fatality rate of around 0.1 percent in non-endemic areas. Pre-exposure vaccination is available for high-risk individuals via local health centres. Macau residents assessed as high risk can receive the vaccine free of charge, while non-resident workers or those legally permitted to stay in Macau may receive paid shots, while tourists remain ineligible. *In late 2022, the World Health Organisation (WHO) recommended transitioning from “monkeypox” to “mpox” to mitigate racist and stigmatising language online, as well as to prevent inaccurate associations with monkeys (rodents are actually the main primary reservoir). – Gemini This image downloaded from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) shows the symptoms of mpox

The two-dose vaccine is strongly encouraged for people at risk. This year, more than 70 mpox cases have been reported in San Francisco as of Aug. 24, according to health officials. Anyone can get mpox, but most reported cases in the United States are among gay, bisexual and other men who have sex with men, as well as transgender persons who have sex with men. “While we are in a much better place than we were during the 2022 outbreak, mpox infections can and still do occur," said San Francisco Health Officer Dr. Susan Philip in a news release. "SFDPH wants people to have a fun and healthy Folsom Street Fair weekend. We strongly encourage people at risk of getting mpox to know the symptoms and be fully vaccinated. As of August 24, more than 70 mpox cases have been reported in the city, highlighting the ongoing risk of the virus. The San Francisco Department of Public Health emphasized that while the situation has improved compared to the 2022 outbreak, mpox infections can still occur. They strongly recommend vaccination for those in high-risk groups, particularly men who have sex with men and transgender individuals who have sex with men. The vaccine is available through healthcare providers and local pharmacies, with additional support for those without insurance. Officials also encourage individuals to be aware of mpox symptoms, which include fever, swollen lymph nodes, fatigue, and a rash resembling pimples or blisters. The recommendation aims to ensure a safe and healthy Folsom Street Fair weekend for attendees.

The sexual health organisation has teamed up with Invisible Boys author Holden Sheppard for their latest video. And it delivers some very unique and cheeky one liners. Mpox Vaccinsations at Perth Steamworks Earlier this year, we reported that MPox cases were on the rise in Western Australia after data released indicated that current cases to date in 2026 have exceeded all of those in 2025. In response, WAAC (formerly the Western Australia Aids Council) is reaching out to the community to encourage everyone to get vaccinated. Launching on their Instagram this week, the organisation dropped their latest public health announcement via video, taking a light-hearted approach to the serious medical issue. “Dragging your feet when it comes to mpox? @holdensheppard is here to tell YOU why you should stop being a drongo and why getting vaccinated for mpox is important for you, your s*x life, and your health” they wrote. Holden Sheppard leads the video, introducing himself as an “award winning author, non award winning labourer and notorious homosexual” as he makes his way to the local sex on premises venue, Perth Steam Works. The video cleverly targets men who are on the “down low” and who may not be out publicly to friends and family, reminding them of the transmission of Mpox through skin-to-skin contact. Sheppard is joined in the video by local Dr Daniel Vujcich, who reminds viewers they simply need to vaccination needles, 28 days apart. “Some guys complete that they don’t like needles. But we know that the guys who come her can handle getting poked” Sheppard quips as he stands in the change room encouraging people to get their jabs. The video goes on to detail that Perth Steam Works also hosts free medical appointments, including vaccinations on site, twice per week, Mondays from 12-2pm or Thursdays from 5.30-7.30pm. Sheppard ends the video hilariously reminding everyone, next time they head to the “vegemite valley,” to head on in and “get a couple of pricks up ya” at the Perth Steam Works. File photo People with multiple sexual partners are at higher risk of infection, according to risk assessment The monkeypox disease does not spread easily between people, the EU health agency said on Monday. "Human-to-human transmission occurs through close contact with infectious material from skin lesions of an infected person, through respiratory droplets in prolonged face-to-face contact, and through fomites," the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) stated in a risk assessment after an outbreak of the illness in non-endemic countries. The report pointed out that most patients diagnosed with monkeypox in Europe were gay men and "the nature of the presenting lesions in some cases, suggest transmission occurred during sexual intercourse." The EU health agency warned that people who have multiple sexual partners are at higher risk of infection. According to the risk assessment, patients have so far only presented mild symptoms during the current outbreak. But, it warned that monkeypox, in general, could cause severe disease. The ECDC recommended EU member states require monkeypox patients to remain isolated and avoid close physical contact until their rash heals completely. Patients can recover at home with supportive care, the document adds. Close contacts of monkeypox patients should observe symptoms carefully for 21 days and refrain from donating blood, organs, or bone marrow. Since the beginning of May, several monkeypox cases have been detected in nine EU countries: Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Italy, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, and the Netherlands. Monkeypox is a virus transmitted to humans from animals, with symptoms including fever, rash, and swollen lymph nodes. news.content: Close Menu Facebook X (Twitter) Instagram Facebook Instagram Threads Subscribe Featured Ebola Outbreak Avian Influenza Measles Resurgence Vaccine News Events Advertisement Contracts + Grants Kansas State’s Zoonotic Disease Research Hub Lands $11.4 Million NIH Renewal Six years of momentum: K-State's infectious disease center enters its next phase By Global Biodefense StaffAugust 29, 2026 Kansas State University researchers examine a sample as part of the university's Center on Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases (CEZID), which recently secured $11.4 million in continued NIH funding through 2031. The center, directed by Juergen A. Richt, studies high-consequence pathogens including H5N1 avian influenza, African swine fever, mpox, and SARS-CoV-2. Photo credit: K-State University. Share Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Email The boundary between animal health and human health has never been more consequential. Diseases that jump from animals to people, from H5N1 avian influenza spreading through dairy cattle to emerging bacterial threats, represent one of the most persistent and unpredictable challenges in global public health. Sustained institutional capacity to study these pathogens before they become crises is exactly what federal research investment is meant to build. Kansas State University has secured $11.4 million in continued National Institutes of Health funding to support the Center on Emerging and Zoonotic Infectious Diseases (CEZID), through April 2031. The NIH award extends the center into its second five-year phase and signals confidence in the research infrastructure and scientific pipeline K-State has built since CEZID launched in 2020. CEZID is housed in K-State’s College of Veterinary Medicine and directed by Juergen A. Richt, a Regents and university distinguished professor whose work spans high-consequence pathogens including H5N1 influenza, African swine fever virus, mpox, and SARS-CoV-2. The center’s mission is straightforward: build the scientific workforce and shared laboratory infrastructure needed to understand how dangerous pathogens cause disease, how they move between animals and humans, and how they can be stopped. K-State sits within a major agricultural corridor and operates some of the country’s most capable high-containment research facilities, including the Biosecurity Research Institute, a BSL-3 and agricultural BSL-3 facility on the Manhattan campus. The nearby National Bio and Agro-Defense Facility further concentrates expertise and infrastructure in the region. CEZID links the university’s infectious disease research to this broader ecosystem, creating a regional hub with national reach. In its first five years, CEZID investigators submitted over 100 research proposals and received 30 awards totaling approximately $18 million in external funding. Phase 2 will pursue four research tracks examining virulence factors and host-pathogen interactions across a range of pathogens. Current projects include studies of Borrelia burgdorferi, the bacterium responsible for Lyme disease; how obesity alters influenza severity through multi-omics analysis; sporulation mechanisms in Clostridioides difficile, a major source of hospital-acquired infection; and a novel coronavirus vaccine strategy using genetic deoptimization to render viruses harmless. Two shared laboratory cores will continue operating throughout Phase 2. The Animal Model/Pathology Core provides BSL-2 and BSL-3 research capabilities, animal model development, and pathology expertise. The Molecular and Cellular Biology Core offers next-generation sequencing, flow cytometry, and spatial transcriptomics. Both cores were integrated into K-State’s Biomedical Core Facilities during Phase 1, extending access to investigators across the university and the broader regional research community. The Regional Scientific Network, which connects CEZID investigators with collaborators at the University of Kansas and the University of Kansas Medical Center, will expand as well. The ongoing H5N1 situation in U.S. dairy herds, which CEZID researchers have studied directly, illustrates how quickly an animal health problem can become a potential human health emergency. The five-year renewal ensures K-State retains and deepens one of the country’s more capable regional centers for this work. Sources and further information: CEZID receives $11.4 million in continued NIH funding – K-State Today This content was researched and sourced by Global Biodefense editors and reported with Claude AI assistance for drafting and editing. 本港今日(29日)新增一宗猴痘确诊个案。卫生署卫生防护中心表示,一名39岁未曾接种猴痘疫苗的男子,于潜伏期内曾与两名陌生男子发生高风险接触,其后出现发烧及全身出疹等症状,检测后证实对猴痘病毒呈阳性反应,目前在玛嘉烈医院隔离治疗,情况稳定。防护中心正进行流行病学调查,并尝试追踪相关接触者。 卫生署卫生防护中心。(资料图片) 卫生防护中心指,该名39岁男子自8月24日起出现发烧及颈部淋巴结肿大,其后口腔出现溃疡,面部、躯干、四肢及生殖器官亦陆续出疹。他于8月26日因自身疾病前往伊利沙伯医院覆诊,即日被安排留院隔离及接受治疗。病人经公共卫生化验服务处采样检测后,今日证实确诊猴痘,并于同日转送至玛嘉烈医院继续接受隔离治疗。 流行病学调查显示,该名病人於潜伏期内曾在本港与两名陌生男子有高风险接触。防护中心指,暂未有资料显示今次个案与本港早前录得的其他猴痘确诊个案存在流行病学关连,中心正全力追查及联系曾与其有高风险接触的人士,并会将个案通报世界卫生组织。 防护中心资料显示,本港自2022年至今累计录得97宗猴痘个案,包括77宗本地个案及20宗输入个案,所有患者均为男性。调查亦发现绝大部份个案均曾进行高风险性行为,包括与陌生人发生性行为,或在没有使用安全套的情况下进行性行为。 猴痘:图为美联社发布日期为2022年5月20日的照片,显示1997年刚果民主共和国一名猴痘病人的手部皮肤状况。(AP) 卫生署呼吁高风险目标群组,包括拥有多名性伴侣、性工作者或过去12个月有性传播感染史的人士尽快接种猴痘疫苗。相关人士可直接前往卫生署辖下的社会卫生科诊所或油麻地综合治疗中心接种,无须预约;九龙湾综合治疗中心以及伊利沙伯医院和玛嘉烈医院的特别内科诊所亦会为到诊者提供接种服务。 当局提醒,猴痘一般不会经空气、飞沫或日常社交接触传播。市民若发现皮疹、发烧、发冷、淋巴结肿大、疲乏或肌肉痛等猴痘症状,应尽快求医,并停止参与任何可能接触到皮疹或体液的活动。 猴痘|39岁男确诊 潜伏期曾在泰国与陌生男子高风险接触猴痘|32岁男确诊 潜伏期曾在港与多名陌生男子有高风险性行为猴痘|31岁男确诊 潜伏期曾在港与多名陌生男子有性行为猴痘|41岁本港男子确诊
